cards.title: Percent means 'per hundred'
cards.body: x% of y = x × y / 100. Memorise fraction equivalents so you can skip long division in the exam.

cards.title: Percentage change
points: % change = (new − old) / old × 100
Successive changes a% then b%: net = a + b + ab/100 (use minus sign for decrease)
Price up r% → cut consumption by r/(100 + r) × 100 % to keep spending same

cards.title: Profit & loss
points: Profit = SP − CP;  Profit% = Profit / CP × 100
SP = MP × (100 − Discount%) / 100
Profit/loss % is on CP; discount % is on Marked Price (MP)

cards.title: Mark-up then discount
cards.body: An item is marked 40% above cost and sold at a 20% discount. Take CP = 100 → MP = 140 → SP = 140 × 0.8 = 112. Profit = 12%. Shortcut: 40 − 20 + (40 × −20)/100 = 12%.

cards.title: Dishonest dealer
cards.body: A dealer sells at cost price but uses a 900 g weight for 1 kg. He gives 900 g, charges for 1000 g. Gain% = 100/900 × 100 = 11.11%.

cards.title: Assume 100
cards.body: Whenever no actual value is given, set CP (or the original quantity) to 100. Every percentage then becomes a plain number, and successive changes are quick to chain.

cards.q: A price rises 20% and then falls 20%. The net change is:
Selling an article for ₹960 gives a 20% profit. What is its cost price?
A's salary is 25% more than B's. By what percent is B's salary less than A's?
cards.explain: Let B = 100, A = 125. Difference 25 on base 125 = 20%.

notes.h: Percent is just a fraction of 100
notes.p:
**Percent** means 'per hundred', so 25% = 25/100 = 1/4. The fastest aptitude solvers do not calculate percentages; they convert them into **fractions** they already know: 10% = 1/10, 12.5% = 1/8, 16.67% = 1/6, 20% = 1/5, 33.33% = 1/3, 37.5% = 3/8, 62.5% = 5/8, 66.67% = 2/3.

To increase a value by r%, multiply by **(1 + r/100)**. To decrease it, multiply by **(1 − r/100)**. So a 20% rise means ×1.2 and a 15% fall means ×0.85. Thinking in multipliers makes chains of changes easy.

The base matters. 'A is 25% more than B' uses B as the base, so A = 1.25B. Then B is less than A by 0.25B/1.25B = **20%**, not 25%. This single trap appears in almost every placement test.
points: Successive changes a% and b%: net change = **a + b + ab/100** (use negative signs for decreases).
Price rises by r%, so to keep spending the same, consumption must fall by **r/(100 + r) × 100%**.
Population growth over n years: P × (1 + r/100)^n (same as compound interest).

notes.p:
**Cost price (CP)** is what the seller paid; **selling price (SP)** is what the buyer pays. Profit% and loss% are always calculated on **CP**, unless the question says otherwise. **Marked price (MP)** is the printed price; **discount** is always calculated on MP.

Key links: SP = CP × (1 + profit%/100); SP = MP × (1 − discount%/100). If a trader marks goods x% above CP and gives a y% discount, his net profit% = x − y − xy/100.
points: Profit% = (SP − CP)/CP × 100.
Same SP for two items, one at x% profit and one at x% loss → always an overall **loss of x²/100 %**.
False weights: a trader who gives 900 g instead of 1000 g at cost price gains 100/900 × 100 = **11.11%**.

notes.p:
**Example 1.** The price of sugar rises by 25%. By how much should a family cut consumption so that spending stays the same? Answer: 25/125 × 100 = **20%**.

**Example 2.** A shopkeeper sells an item at a 10% loss. Had he sold it for ₹45 more, he would have gained 5%. Find CP. The gap between −10% and +5% is 15% of CP, so 0.15 × CP = 45 and **CP = ₹300**.

**Example 3.** Goods are marked 20% above CP and sold at a 10% discount. SP = 1.2 × 0.9 × CP = 1.08 CP, so profit = **8%** (check: 20 − 10 − 200/100 = 8).

**Example 4.** Two phones are sold for ₹1,200 each, one at 20% profit and one at 20% loss. CP1 = 1200/1.2 = 1000, CP2 = 1200/0.8 = 1500. Total CP = 2500, total SP = 2400, so the loss is 100/2500 = **4%** (matches 20²/100).

notes.h: Check your answer with a tiny program
notes.p:
If you are preparing for coding rounds too, it helps to model aptitude formulas in code. This function applies a list of percentage changes one after another:

`def net_change(*changes):
    factor = 1
    for c in changes:
        factor *= 1 + c / 100
    return round((factor - 1) * 100, 2)

print(net_change(20, -20))   # +20% then -20%
print(net_change(10, 10))    # two 10% rises
print(net_change(20, -10))   # mark-up 20%, discount 10%`

Output:
`-4.0
21.0
8.0`

**Q: If A's salary is 25% more than B's, by what percent is B's salary less than A's?** A: 25/125 × 100 = 20%.

**Q: A number is increased by 10% and then decreased by 10%. What is the net change?** A: 10 − 10 − 1 = −1%, a 1% decrease, not zero.

**Q: By selling 20 pens, a man gains the cost price of 5 pens. Find gain%.** A: Gain = CP of 5, cost = CP of 20, so 5/20 = 25%.
points: Trap: calculating profit% on SP instead of CP.
Trap: calculating discount on CP instead of MP.
Trap: adding successive percentages directly (20% + 20% is 44%, not 40%).

notes.p: Memorise these before the test:
points: Learn fraction equivalents of 1/2 to 1/12 as percentages.
Increase by r% → ×(1 + r/100); decrease → ×(1 − r/100).
Successive change: a + b + ab/100.
Profit and loss on CP; discount on MP.
Same SP, x% profit and x% loss → x²/100 % loss.
Spending constant: cut consumption by r/(100 + r).
Always re-read which quantity is the base of the percentage.

cards.title: Work as a rate
cards.body: If A finishes a job in n days, A does 1/n of it per day. Rates of people working together simply add; time = total work / combined rate.

cards.title: Core formulas
points: A and B together: time = ab / (a + b)
M1·D1·H1 / W1 = M2·D2·H2 / W2 (men, days, hours, work)
If A is k times as efficient as B, A takes 1/k of B's time

cards.title: LCM method
cards.body: A takes 12 days, B takes 18 days. Let total work = LCM(12, 18) = 36 units. A does 3 units/day, B does 2 units/day. Together 5 units/day → 36/5 = 7.2 days. No fractions needed.

cards.title: Pipes & cisterns
cards.body: Same idea as work: an inlet pipe adds a positive rate, an outlet or leak adds a negative rate. Net rate = sum of inlets − sum of outlets.

cards.title: Fill with an outlet open
cards.body: Pipe A fills a tank in 6 h, pipe B empties it in 8 h. Net per hour = 1/6 − 1/8 = 1/24, so the tank fills in 24 h. LCM way: tank = 24 units, A +4, B −3, net +1 → 24 h.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Always convert to units with LCM. For 'A works for some days, then leaves' questions, subtract the work done so far, then divide the remainder by the remaining rate.

cards.q: A can finish a job in 10 days and B in 15 days. Working together they finish in:
cards.explain: Work = 30 units; A = 3/day, B = 2/day; together 5/day → 30/5 = 6 days.

cards.q: 12 men complete a job in 18 days. How many days will 27 men take?
cards.explain: Man-days are constant: 12 × 18 = 216 = 27 × D → D = 8.

cards.q: A tap fills a tank in 4 h; a leak empties it in 12 h. With both acting, the tank fills in:

notes.p:
If a person finishes a job in **n days**, they do **1/n of the job per day**. Work rates add when people work together: if A takes 10 days and B takes 15 days, together they do 1/10 + 1/15 = 1/6 of the job per day, so they need **6 days**.

A cleaner method used by toppers is the **LCM (total units) method**. Take total work = LCM(10, 15) = 30 units. A does 3 units/day, B does 2 units/day, together 5 units/day, so 30/5 = 6 days. No fractions, fewer mistakes.

**Efficiency** is inversely proportional to time. If A is twice as efficient as B, A takes half the time B takes.
points: Men-days rule: M1 × D1 × H1 / W1 = M2 × D2 × H2 / W2 (M = men, D = days, H = hours per day, W = work).
If A and B together take T days and A alone takes a days, B alone takes aT/(a − T) days.
Wages are shared in the ratio of work done, not in the ratio of days.

notes.p:
Pipes are the same idea with signs. A **filling pipe** adds work (+), an **emptying pipe or leak** subtracts work (−). If a tank is filled by pipe A in 20 min and B in 30 min, and pipe C empties it in 60 min, then per minute: 1/20 + 1/30 − 1/60 = (3 + 2 − 1)/60 = 4/60 = 1/15. All three together fill the tank in **15 minutes**.

**Leak question:** a pipe fills a tank in 6 hours, but because of a leak it takes 8 hours. Leak rate = 1/6 − 1/8 = 1/24, so the leak alone empties a full tank in **24 hours**.

**Example 1.** A and B together finish a job in 12 days. A alone takes 20 days. How long does B take? 1/12 − 1/20 = (5 − 3)/60 = 1/30, so **B takes 30 days**.

**Example 2.** A is twice as efficient as B. Together they finish in 12 days. Let B do 1 unit/day, A 2 units/day. Total = 3 × 12 = 36 units. B alone: **36 days**; A alone: 18 days.

**Example 3.** 12 men build a wall in 10 days. How many days for 15 men? 12 × 10 = 15 × D, so **D = 8 days**.

**Example 4.** A can do a job in 10 days, B in 15. A works for 4 days and leaves. Using 30 units: A does 3 × 4 = 12 units, 18 units remain, B does 2 units/day, so **B needs 9 more days**.

Fractions in Python avoid rounding errors, which is useful when you build your own practice checker:

`from fractions import Fraction as F

def together(*days):
    rate = sum(F(1, d) for d in days)
    return 1 / rate

print(together(10, 15))                 # A and B
print(1 / (F(1, 20) + F(1, 30) - F(1, 60)))  # pipes A, B fill; C empties
print(1 / (F(1, 6) - F(1, 8)))           # leak alone`

Output:
`6
15
24`

**Q: A, B and C can do a work in 6, 12 and 24 days. In how many days will they finish together?** A: Units = 24; rates 4 + 2 + 1 = 7 units/day; 24/7 = 3 3/7 days.

**Q: A and B earn ₹6,000 for a job; A takes 10 days and B 15 days working together. What is A's share?** A: Work ratio 3 : 2, so A gets ₹3,600.

**Q: Pipe A fills in 4 h and B empties in 6 h. Both open: time to fill?** A: 1/4 − 1/6 = 1/12, so 12 hours.
points: Trap: averaging days (10 and 15 do not give 12.5 days together).
Trap: forgetting the minus sign for leaks and outlet pipes.
Trap: alternate-day questions (A on day 1, B on day 2) need cycle-by-cycle counting near the end.

notes.p: Five-minute recap:
points: Rate = 1/time; rates add, times do not.
Use total units = LCM of the given times.
Efficiency ratio is the inverse of the time ratio.
M1D1H1/W1 = M2D2H2/W2.
Inlet pipe +, outlet pipe or leak −.
Wages split by work done.

cards.title: Basics and units
cards.body: Distance = Speed × Time. Convert units first.
points: km/h → m/s: multiply by 5/18
m/s → km/h: multiply by 18/5

cards.title: Average speed
points: Average speed = total distance / total time
Equal distances at x and y: 2xy / (x + y)
Equal times at x and y: (x + y) / 2

cards.title: Relative speed
cards.body: Two bodies moving in the same direction: relative speed = difference of speeds. Opposite directions: sum of speeds. Use relative speed for meeting and overtaking questions.

cards.title: Trains
points: Cross a pole/person: time = train length / speed
Cross a platform/bridge: (train + platform length) / speed
Two trains crossing: (L1 + L2) / relative speed

cards.title: Boats & streams
points: Downstream speed D = u + v; upstream U = u − v
Boat speed in still water u = (D + U)/2
Stream speed v = (D − U)/2

cards.title: Train example
cards.body: A 150 m train runs at 54 km/h = 15 m/s. It crosses a pole in 150/15 = 10 s and a 300 m platform in (150 + 300)/15 = 30 s.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Never average the two speeds for a round trip; use 2xy/(x + y). Write all units in m and s (or km and h) before substituting.

cards.q: A car goes from A to B at 40 km/h and returns at 60 km/h. Average speed for the round trip?
72 km/h equals:
A boat goes 16 km/h downstream and 10 km/h upstream. Speed of the stream?
cards.explain: Stream = (16 − 10)/2 = 3 km/h. (Boat = 13 km/h.)

notes.p:
**Distance = Speed × Time.** Keep the units consistent. To convert **km/h to m/s multiply by 5/18**; to convert m/s to km/h multiply by 18/5. So 54 km/h = 15 m/s and 36 km/h = 10 m/s.

For a fixed distance, speed and time are **inversely proportional**. If speed becomes 4/3 of the original, time becomes 3/4 of the original, which is how many 'reaches 15 minutes early' questions are solved.

**Average speed** = total distance / total time. It is not the average of the speeds. For two equal distances at speeds x and y, average speed = **2xy/(x + y)**. Going at 40 km/h and returning at 60 km/h gives 2 × 40 × 60/100 = 48 km/h.

When two objects move in **opposite directions**, relative speed = sum of speeds. In the **same direction**, relative speed = difference. A train crossing a pole or a standing man covers its **own length**; crossing a platform or another train covers the **sum of lengths**.

Boats and streams: with boat speed u in still water and stream speed v, **downstream = u + v** and **upstream = u − v**. So u = (down + up)/2 and v = (down − up)/2.

Circular track: two runners starting together meet for the first time after track length / relative speed.

**Example 1.** A 150 m train runs at 54 km/h (15 m/s). Time to cross a pole = 150/15 = **10 s**. Time to cross a 300 m platform = 450/15 = **30 s**.

**Example 2.** Trains of 100 m and 150 m run in opposite directions at 36 and 54 km/h. Relative speed = 90 km/h = 25 m/s. Time to cross = 250/25 = **10 s**. In the same direction, relative speed = 18 km/h = 5 m/s, time = **50 s**.

**Example 3.** A boat goes 10 km/h in still water; the stream flows at 2 km/h. A 24 km trip downstream and back takes 24/12 + 24/8 = 2 + 3 = **5 hours**.

**Example 4.** Walking at 4 km/h a student is 10 min late; at 5 km/h he is 5 min early. The time difference is 15 min = 1/4 h. d/4 − d/5 = 1/4 gives d/20 = 1/4, so **d = 5 km**.

**Example 5.** Two runners on a 360 m circular track run in opposite directions at 5 m/s and 7 m/s. They meet every 360/12 = **30 s**.

`def kmph_to_mps(v):
    return v * 5 / 18

def cross_time(len1, len2, s1, s2, same_dir):
    rel = abs(s1 - s2) if same_dir else s1 + s2
    return (len1 + len2) / kmph_to_mps(rel)

print(cross_time(100, 150, 36, 54, False))
print(cross_time(100, 150, 36, 54, True))
print(2 * 40 * 60 / (40 + 60))`

Output:
`10.0
50.0
48.0`

**Q: A car covers half the distance at 30 km/h and half at 60 km/h. Average speed?** A: 2 × 30 × 60/90 = 40 km/h.

**Q: A train passes a man walking at 6 km/h in the same direction in 9 s. Train speed is 66 km/h. Length?** A: Relative speed 60 km/h = 50/3 m/s; length = 50/3 × 9 = 150 m.

**Q: Downstream speed 16 km/h, upstream 10 km/h. Stream speed?** A: (16 − 10)/2 = 3 km/h.
points: Trap: mixing km/h with metres and seconds.
Trap: taking the simple average of speeds.
Trap: forgetting to add the platform length.

notes.p: Remember:
points: D = S × T; km/h × 5/18 = m/s.
Average speed for equal distances = 2xy/(x + y).
Opposite directions add speeds; same direction subtract.
Train crossing pole = own length; platform/train = sum of lengths.
Downstream u + v, upstream u − v.
Fixed distance: speed ratio a : b means time ratio b : a.

cards.title: Counting principle
cards.body: If one task can be done in m ways AND a second in n ways, together: m × n. If it is one task OR the other: m + n.

cards.title: Core formulas
points: nPr = n! / (n − r)!  (order matters)
nCr = n! / (r! (n − r)!)  (selection, order doesn't matter)
nCr = nC(n−r); 0! = 1
Arrangements with repeats: n! / (p! q! …)
Circular arrangement: (n − 1)!; necklace/garland: (n − 1)!/2

cards.title: Repeated letters
cards.body: LEVEL has 5 letters with L×2 and E×2. Arrangements = 5! / (2! × 2!) = 120 / 4 = 30.

cards.title: Probability
cards.body: P(E) = favourable outcomes / total equally likely outcomes. P(not E) = 1 − P(E). For independent events P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B); P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B).

cards.title: Cards
cards.body: P(king or heart) from 52 cards = 4/52 + 13/52 − 1/52 (king of hearts counted twice) = 16/52 = 4/13.

cards.title: 'At least one' trick
cards.body: P(at least one) = 1 − P(none). Example: at least one head in 3 tosses = 1 − (1/2)³ = 7/8.

cards.q: In how many ways can the letters of APPLE be arranged?
cards.explain: 5 letters, P repeats twice: 5!/2! = 120/2 = 60.

cards.q: A committee of 3 is chosen from 5 people. Number of ways?
cards.explain: 5C3 = 5!/(3!·2!) = 10. Order does not matter, so it is a combination.

cards.q: Three fair coins are tossed. Probability of at least one head?

notes.h: Counting: when order matters and when it does not
notes.p:
The **fundamental counting principle** says: if one task can be done in m ways and another in n ways, both together can be done in **m × n** ways (AND → multiply, OR → add).

**Permutation** (order matters, arrangements): nPr = n!/(n − r)!. **Combination** (order does not matter, selections): nCr = n!/(r!(n − r)!). Ask yourself: 'If I swap two chosen items, is it a new outcome?' If yes, use permutation.

Repeated letters: arrangements of a word with n letters where one letter repeats p times and another q times = **n!/(p! q!)**. Circular arrangements of n distinct people = **(n − 1)!**; if clockwise and anticlockwise are the same (necklace), divide by 2.
points: nC0 = nCn = 1 and nCr = nC(n − r).
'At least one' = total − none.
Items always together: tie them into one block, then multiply by their internal arrangements.

notes.p:
**Probability = favourable outcomes / total equally likely outcomes**, always between 0 and 1. P(not A) = 1 − P(A). For **independent** events P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B). For any two events P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B).

Standard sample spaces: one die has 6 outcomes, two dice 36, three coins 8, a deck 52 cards (4 suits of 13; 12 face cards; 4 aces).

**Example 1.** Arrangements of BANANA: 6 letters, A three times, N twice: 6!/(3! 2!) = 720/12 = **60**.

**Example 2.** A committee of 3 men from 5 and 2 women from 4: 5C3 × 4C2 = 10 × 6 = **60**.

**Example 3.** Six friends around a round table: (6 − 1)! = **120**.

**Example 4.** Two dice: P(sum = 7). Favourable pairs (1,6), (2,5), (3,4), (4,3), (5,2), (6,1) = 6, so 6/36 = **1/6**.

**Example 5.** A bag has 5 red and 3 blue balls. Two are drawn without replacement. P(both red) = 5C2/8C2 = 10/28 = **5/14**.

**Example 6.** P(at least one head in 3 tosses) = 1 − 1/8 = **7/8**.

In a test you use formulas, but while practising you can confirm answers by listing every outcome:

`from itertools import permutations, product
from math import comb, perm
from fractions import Fraction

print(len(set(permutations("BANANA"))))
print(comb(5, 3) * comb(4, 2), perm(5, 2))
dice = list(product(range(1, 7), repeat=2))
print(Fraction(sum(1 for a, b in dice if a + b == 7), len(dice)))
print(Fraction(comb(5, 2), comb(8, 2)))`

Output:
`60
60 20
1/6
5/14`

**Q: In how many ways can the letters of LEADER be arranged?** A: 6 letters, E twice: 6!/2! = 360.

**Q: How many 3-digit numbers can be formed from 1–5 without repetition?** A: 5 × 4 × 3 = 60.

**Q: A card is drawn from a deck. P(king or heart)?** A: 4/52 + 13/52 − 1/52 = 16/52 = 4/13.
points: Trap: using permutation for a committee (order does not matter).
Trap: counting the king of hearts twice in 'king or heart'.
Trap: 'with replacement' vs 'without replacement' changes the denominator.
Trap: a 3-digit number cannot start with 0.

notes.p: Formula sheet:
points: nPr = n!/(n − r)!, nCr = n!/(r!(n − r)!).
Repeated letters: n!/(p! q! …).
Circular: (n − 1)!; necklace: (n − 1)!/2.
AND → multiply, OR → add.
P(at least one) = 1 − P(none).
P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B).

cards.title: Divisibility rules
points: 3 / 9: sum of digits divisible by 3 / 9
4: last two digits; 8: last three digits
11: (sum of odd-place digits − sum of even-place digits) is 0 or a multiple of 11
6: divisible by both 2 and 3

cards.title: HCF & LCM
points: HCF × LCM = product of the two numbers
HCF of fractions = HCF of numerators / LCM of denominators
LCM of fractions = LCM of numerators / HCF of denominators

cards.title: Unit digit cyclicity
cards.body: Powers repeat their last digit in cycles of 4 (or less). Find exponent mod 4; remainder 0 means take the 4th term.

cards.title: Unit digit of 7^95
cards.body: 95 mod 4 = 3 → third term of the cycle 7, 9, 3, 1 → unit digit is 3.

cards.title: Trailing zeros of n!
cards.body: Count factors of 5: ⌊n/5⌋ + ⌊n/25⌋ + ⌊n/125⌋ + … Example: 100! → 20 + 4 = 24 zeros.

cards.title: Remainders
cards.body: (a × b) mod n = ((a mod n) × (b mod n)) mod n, and the same for +. Example: 17 × 23 mod 5 = (2 × 3) mod 5 = 1.

cards.title: Number of factors
cards.body: Write N = p^a · q^b · r^c. Factors = (a+1)(b+1)(c+1). Example: 72 = 2³ · 3² → 4 × 3 = 12 factors.

cards.q: Unit digit of 3^65?
cards.explain: 65 mod 4 = 1 → first term of 3, 9, 7, 1 → 3.

cards.q: Number of trailing zeros in 50!:
HCF of two numbers is 12, LCM is 180 and one number is 36. The other is:

notes.p:
**Natural numbers** start at 1, **whole numbers** at 0, **integers** include negatives. A **prime** has exactly two factors (1 is not prime; 2 is the only even prime). **Co-primes** have HCF 1, like 8 and 15.

Divisibility shortcuts: by 3 or 9 → digit sum divisible by 3 or 9; by 4 → last two digits; by 8 → last three digits; by 11 → (sum of odd-place digits − sum of even-place digits) is 0 or a multiple of 11; by 6 → by 2 and 3.
points: Number of factors of N = p^a × q^b × r^c is **(a + 1)(b + 1)(c + 1)**.
HCF × LCM = product of the two numbers (only for two numbers).
HCF of fractions = HCF(numerators)/LCM(denominators); LCM of fractions = LCM(numerators)/HCF(denominators).

notes.h: Remainders, unit digits and trailing zeros
notes.p:
**Unit digit cycles:** powers of 2 cycle 2, 4, 8, 6; of 3 cycle 3, 9, 7, 1; of 7 cycle 7, 9, 3, 1; of 8 cycle 8, 4, 2, 6. Digits 0, 1, 5, 6 always repeat themselves. Divide the power by 4 and use the remainder (remainder 0 means the 4th term).

**Remainder tricks:** find a small power that gives remainder 1. For 2^100 mod 7, note 2^3 = 8 ≡ 1 (mod 7). 100 = 3 × 33 + 1, so 2^100 ≡ 2^1 = **2**.

**Trailing zeros in n!** = ⌊n/5⌋ + ⌊n/25⌋ + ⌊n/125⌋ + … because each zero needs a pair (2, 5) and 5s are rarer. For 100!: 20 + 4 = **24**.

**Example 1.** Number of factors of 360 = 2³ × 3² × 5¹ → (3 + 1)(2 + 1)(1 + 1) = **24**.

**Example 2.** Unit digit of 7^95: 95 mod 4 = 3, third term of (7, 9, 3, 1) is **3**.

**Example 3.** Largest 4-digit number divisible by 88: 9999 mod 88 = 55, so 9999 − 55 = **9944**.

**Example 4.** Two numbers have HCF 12 and LCM 360. One is 60. The other = 12 × 360/60 = **72**.

Python's built-in three-argument `pow(base, exp, mod)` computes remainders of huge powers instantly:

`from math import gcd

def zeros_in_factorial(n):
    count, p = 0, 5
    while p <= n:
        count += n // p
        p *= 5
    return count

def num_factors(n):
    return sum(1 for d in range(1, n + 1) if n % d == 0)

print(pow(2, 100, 7), pow(7, 95, 10))
print(zeros_in_factorial(100), num_factors(360))
print(9999 - 9999 % 88, 12 * 360 // 60, gcd(60, 72))`

Output:
`2 3
24 24
9944 72 12`

**Q: What is the remainder when 17^23 is divided by 16?** A: 17 ≡ 1 (mod 16), so 1^23 = 1.

**Q: How many prime numbers are there between 1 and 50?** A: 15.

**Q: Find the least number which leaves remainder 3 when divided by 4, 6 and 9.** A: LCM(4, 6, 9) + 3 = 36 + 3 = 39.
points: Trap: treating 1 as prime.
Trap: using HCF × LCM = product for three numbers (it does not hold).
Trap: unit-digit cycle with remainder 0 means the 4th value, not the first.

notes.p: Keep in mind:
points: Divisibility rules for 2–11.
Factor count = product of (exponent + 1).
Unit digits repeat every 4 powers.
Trailing zeros: divide by 5, 25, 125 …
Find a power ≡ 1 to reduce big remainders.
HCF × LCM = a × b for two numbers.

cards.title: Ratios
cards.body: To combine A:B and B:C, make B equal. A:B = 2:3 and B:C = 4:5 → scale to 8:12 and 12:15 → A:B:C = 8:12:15.

cards.title: Averages
cards.body: Average = sum / count. When an item is removed or replaced, work with sums, not averages. New sum − old sum tells you the value added or removed.

cards.title: Interest
points: Simple interest SI = P × R × T / 100
Compound amount A = P (1 + R/100)^T; CI = A − P
CI − SI for 2 years = P (R/100)²

cards.title: Alligation
cards.body: Mixing a cheaper and a dearer item to get a mean price: cheaper qty : dearer qty = (dearer − mean) : (mean − cheaper).

cards.title: Alligation example
cards.body: Rice at ₹20/kg and ₹30/kg mixed to sell at ₹24/kg cost. Ratio = (30 − 24) : (24 − 20) = 6 : 4 = 3 : 2.

cards.q: The average of 5 numbers is 20. One number is removed and the average becomes 18. The removed number is:
cards.explain: Old sum 100; new sum 4 × 18 = 72; removed = 28.

cards.q: Simple interest on ₹5,000 at 8% p.a. for 3 years:
A:B = 2:3 and B:C = 4:5. Find A:B:C.

notes.p:
A **ratio** a : b compares two quantities of the same kind. To combine chained ratios, make the common term equal: if A : B = 2 : 3 and B : C = 4 : 5, multiply the first by 4 and the second by 3 to get A : B : C = **8 : 12 : 15**.

To split an amount in ratio a : b, A gets a/(a + b) of it. In **partnership**, profit is shared in the ratio of **capital × time**.

**Average = sum/count**. If one item is removed or added, work with the totals, not the averages. If the average of 5 numbers is 20 and it becomes 18 after removing one, the removed number = 100 − 72 = **28**.

**Alligation** gives the ratio in which two ingredients at prices c (cheaper) and d (dearer) must be mixed to get mean price m: **cheaper : dearer = (d − m) : (m − c)**. Rice at ₹20/kg and ₹30/kg mixed to get ₹24/kg → (30 − 24) : (24 − 20) = 6 : 4 = **3 : 2**.

Mixture example: 40 L of milk and water in ratio 3 : 1 contains 30 L milk and 10 L water. To make the ratio 3 : 2, water must be 20 L, so **add 10 L of water**.

**Simple interest:** SI = P × R × T/100. Interest is the same every year. **Compound interest:** amount A = P(1 + R/100)^T and CI = A − P. Interest is earned on interest.

For P = ₹10,000 at 10% for 2 years: SI = ₹2,000; A = 10000 × 1.21 = ₹12,100 so CI = ₹2,100. The difference CI − SI for 2 years = **P(R/100)²** = 10000 × 0.01 = ₹100.

Half-yearly compounding: use R/2 per period and 2T periods.
points: Sum doubles in T years at SI → R = 100/T.
Rule of 72: at R% compound interest, money roughly doubles in 72/R years.

notes.p:
`P, R, T = 10000, 10, 2
si = P * R * T / 100
ci = P * pow(1 + R / 100, T) - P
print(si, round(ci, 2), round(ci - si, 2))

def alligation(cheap, dear, mean):
    return (dear - mean), (mean - cheap)
print(alligation(20, 30, 24))
print((5 * 20 - 4 * 18))`

Output:
`2000.0 2100.0 100.0
(6, 4)
28`

**Q: A and B invest ₹20,000 and ₹30,000; A stays 12 months, B 8 months. Ratio of profit?** A: 2,40,000 : 2,40,000 = 1 : 1.

**Q: The average age of 30 students is 15. If the teacher is included, it becomes 16. Teacher's age?** A: 31 × 16 − 30 × 15 = 496 − 450 = 46.

**Q: At what SI rate does a sum double in 8 years?** A: 100/8 = 12.5%.
points: Trap: adding ratios from different bases without equalising the common term.
Trap: averaging averages of groups with different sizes (use weighted average).
Trap: forgetting to halve the rate for half-yearly compounding.

notes.p: Summary:
points: Chain ratios by equalising the middle term.
Partnership: capital × time.
Work with totals when averages change.
Alligation: (d − m) : (m − c).
CI − SI for 2 years = P(R/100)².

cards.title: Clock basics
points: Minute hand: 6° per minute; hour hand: 0.5° per minute (30° per hour)
Relative speed: 5.5° per minute
Angle at H:M = |30H − 5.5M| (use 360 − θ if θ > 180)
Hands coincide every 720/11 = 65 5⁄11 minutes

cards.title: Counts in a day (24 h)
points: Hands coincide 22 times
Hands are at right angles 44 times
Hands point in opposite directions 22 times
Between H and H+1 they coincide at 60H/11 minutes past H

cards.title: Angle at 3:40
cards.body: θ = |30 × 3 − 5.5 × 40| = |90 − 220| = **130°**. The reflex angle is 230°; the question normally wants the smaller one.

cards.title: Odd days
points: Odd days = days beyond complete weeks
Ordinary year: 365 = 52 weeks + 1 → 1 odd day; leap year → 2
Leap year: divisible by 4, but century years only if divisible by 400 (1900 no, 2000 yes)

cards.title: Day codes
cards.body: Count odd days from a known reference, then map 0 = Sunday, 1 = Monday, …, 6 = Saturday. Month odd days in an ordinary year: Jan 3, Feb 0, Mar 3, Apr 2, May 3, Jun 2, Jul 3, Aug 3, Sep 2, Oct 3, Nov 2, Dec 3 (Feb 1 in a leap year).

cards.title: Repeating calendars
cards.body: Two years have identical calendars when they start on the same weekday and are both leap or both ordinary. A leap-year calendar repeats after 28 years (within a century with normal leap years). An ordinary year's calendar repeats after 6 or 11 years — e.g. 2023 → 2034, 2025 → 2031.

cards.q: The angle between the hands at 7:20 is:
At what time between 4 and 5 o'clock do the hands coincide?
Which of these is NOT a leap year?
cards.explain: 1900 is a century year not divisible by 400.

notes.p:
In M minutes past H o'clock, the hour hand is at 30H + 0.5M degrees from 12 and the minute hand at 6M. The difference is |30H − 5.5M|. Every 'when are the hands at angle θ' question solves |30H − 5.5M| = θ for M, giving two answers per hour for most θ (one before and one after the hands meet).

**Worked example 1.** When between 2 and 3 are the hands at right angles? |60 − 5.5M| = 90 → M = 150/5.5 = **27 3⁄11** min (the other root, 60 − 5.5M = 90, gives a negative M). In some hours both roots are valid; here only one is.

If a clock gains g minutes in every 60 real minutes, it shows 60 + g minutes when 60 real minutes pass. **Worked example 2.** A clock set right at 8:00 a.m. gains 5 minutes every hour. What is the real time when it shows 2:00 p.m. the same day? It has shown 6 hours = 360 minutes; real minutes = 360 × 60/65 ≈ 332.3 = 5 h 32 4⁄13 min → real time ≈ **1:32 p.m.** Always convert using the ratio of real to shown time.

notes.h: Calendar method and check with code
notes.p:
`import datetime as d, calendar
print(d.date(1950, 1, 26).strftime('%A'), d.date(1947, 8, 15).strftime('%A'))
print(calendar.isleap(1900), calendar.isleap(2000), calendar.isleap(2100))
def same_calendar(y):
    for z in range(y + 1, y + 40):
        if d.date(z, 1, 1).weekday() == d.date(y, 1, 1).weekday() and calendar.isleap(z) == calendar.isleap(y):
            return z
print(same_calendar(2023), same_calendar(2024), same_calendar(2025))
angle = lambda h, m: min(abs(30 * h - 5.5 * m), 360 - abs(30 * h - 5.5 * m))
print(angle(3, 40), angle(7, 20), angle(9, 0))`

Output:
`Thursday Friday
False True False
2034 2052 2031
130.0 100.0 90.0`

**Worked example 3 (by hand).** What day was 26 January 1950? Odd days up to 31 Dec 1949: 1600 years → 0; 300 years → 1; 49 years with 12 leap years → 37 + 24 = 61 → 61 mod 7 = 5. Total = 6. Then 26 days of January → 26 mod 7 = 5. Overall 6 + 5 = 11 → 4 → **Thursday**, matching the code.
Watch out for:
points: Using 6M − 30H without the hour hand's 0.5° per minute drift.
Forgetting that 1900 and 2100 are not leap years.
Counting the start date itself when finding the day after N days.
Taking the reflex angle when the question asks for the angle between hands.

notes.p: Remember:
points: θ = |30H − 5.5M|; take 360 − θ if over 180.
Coincide every 65 5⁄11 min; 22 times a day.
Right angles 44 times a day; opposite 22 times.
Ordinary year 1 odd day, leap year 2.
Century leap year only if divisible by 400.
0 = Sunday … 6 = Saturday.

cards.title: Alligation rule
points: Cheaper : dearer = (d − m) : (m − c)
c = cheaper value, d = dearer value, m = mean (mixture) value
Works for prices, concentrations, speeds, marks — any weighted average of two groups

cards.title: Repeated replacement
points: Vessel of V litres of pure liquid; remove x litres and refill with water, n times
Pure liquid left = V × (1 − x/V)ⁿ
Concentration after n operations = (1 − x/V)ⁿ of the original

cards.title: Replacement
cards.body:
40 L of milk; 4 L removed and replaced with water, three times.
Milk left = 40 × (36/40)³ = 40 × 0.729 = **29.16 L**.

cards.title: Mixing two mixtures
cards.body:
Vessel A has milk : water = 3 : 1 (75% milk); vessel B has 2 : 3 (40% milk). Target 1 : 1 (50% milk).
A : B = (50 − 40) : (75 − 50) = 10 : 25 = **2 : 5**.

cards.title: Adding to change a ratio
cards.body: Keep the quantity that does **not** change fixed. 60 L of milk and water in ratio 2 : 1 has 40 L milk and 20 L water. To make it 1 : 2, water must be 80 L → add **60 L** of water. Milk never changed, so it anchors the calculation.

cards.title: Dishonest milkman
cards.body: Selling a water–milk mixture at the cost price of milk gives profit % = water/milk × 100. For a 25% profit he mixes water : milk = **1 : 4**. If he also marks up the price, combine the two effects multiplicatively.

cards.q: Rice at ₹30/kg and ₹45/kg is mixed to sell at ₹36/kg (no profit). The mixing ratio cheap : dear is:
A 50 L vessel of pure juice: 5 L is replaced with water twice. Juice remaining:
A milkman wants 20% profit by adding water and selling at the cost price of milk. Water : milk =
cards.explain: Profit % = water/milk × 100 = 20 → 1 : 5.

notes.p: A mixture's value is a **weighted average** of its parts. Alligation is just a shortcut for that weighted average: the mean sits between the two values, closer to the one used in larger quantity. Put the two values on a number line with the mean between them; the distances, swapped, give the ratio. This also solves 'average marks of boys and girls' and 'average speed of two parts of a journey by time'.

**Example 1.** How many litres of a 20% acid solution must be added to 30 L of a 50% solution to get 30%? By alligation 20% : 50% = (50 − 30) : (30 − 20) = 2 : 1, so 20% solution = 2 × 30 = **60 L**.

**Example 2.** A 90 L mixture has milk : water = 7 : 2. How much of it should be replaced with water so that the ratio becomes 7 : 5? Milk = 70 L, water = 20 L. Removing y litres removes 7y/9 milk; new milk = 70 − 7y/9 must be 7/12 of 90 = 52.5 → 7y/9 = 17.5 → y = **22.5 L**.

**Example 3.** Two alloys have gold : copper 5 : 3 and 1 : 3. In what ratio should they be melted to get 1 : 1? Gold fractions 5/8 = 62.5% and 1/4 = 25%; target 50%. Ratio = (50 − 25) : (62.5 − 50) = 25 : 12.5 = **2 : 1**.

`from fractions import Fraction as Fr
def alligation(c, d, m):
    r = Fr(d - m) / Fr(m - c)
    return r.numerator, r.denominator
print(alligation(30, 45, 36), alligation(Fr(2, 5), Fr(3, 4), Fr(1, 2)))
print(40 * (1 - Fr(4, 40)) ** 3, float(40 * (1 - Fr(4, 40)) ** 3))
milk, water = 70, 20
for y in [Fr(45, 2)]:
    m, w = milk - y * Fr(7, 9), water - y * Fr(2, 9) + y
    print(y, m / w)
print(alligation(Fr(1, 4), Fr(5, 8), Fr(1, 2)))`

Output:
`(3, 2) (5, 2)
729/25 29.16
45/2 7/5
(1, 2)`

The helper returns cheaper : dearer — 3 : 2 for the rice, 5 : 2 for B : A (so A : B = 2 : 5), and 1 : 2 for the 25% : 62.5% alloys (so first alloy : second = 2 : 1). Replacing 22.5 L gives milk : water = 7/5 exactly.
Avoid:
points: Applying alligation to ratios of milk : water directly — convert to fractions (or % milk) of the whole first.
Using the replacement formula when the removed liquid is not replaced (then it is a simple ratio).
Forgetting which side is cheaper when writing (d − m) : (m − c).
Adding water changes the total, so recompute percentages on the new total.

notes.p: Remember:
points: Cheaper : dearer = (d − m) : (m − c).
Convert ratios to fractions of the whole before alligating.
Replacement: V(1 − x/V)ⁿ remains.
Anchor on the component that does not change.
Milkman profit % = water/milk × 100.
Alligation = weighted average in disguise.

chapters.title: Data interpretation: tables, bar, line & pie charts

cards.title: What DI tests
cards.body: Reading a table or chart quickly and computing **percentage change, ratios, averages, shares and differences**. Accuracy matters more than speed tricks, but approximation saves time when options are far apart.

cards.title: Core formulas
points: % change = (new − old)/old × 100
Share of a part = part/total × 100
Pie-chart angle = share × 360°
Average = total/count; growth over n years ≈ use (final/initial)^(1/n) − 1 for compound rate
Ratio questions: simplify by the HCF

cards.title: Chart types
cards.body: **Table**: exact values — compute directly. **Bar chart**: compare heights; read the scale carefully. **Line chart**: trends — the steepest segment is the largest absolute change, not necessarily the largest percentage change. **Pie chart**: shares of one total; you need the total to get actual values.

cards.title: Approximation
cards.body: Round to convenient numbers and keep track of the direction of error. 1/7 ≈ 14.3%, 1/8 = 12.5%, 1/9 ≈ 11.1%, 1/11 ≈ 9.1%, 1/12 ≈ 8.3%. When two options differ by less than about 2%, calculate exactly.

cards.title: Highest growth
cards.body: Sales 2022 → 2023: A 50 → 60 (+20%), B 36 → 45 (+25%), C 45 → 54 (+20%), D 25 → 30 (+20%). B has the **highest percentage** growth even though A, B and C all grew by 9–10 units.

cards.title: Read the question twice
cards.body: Questions often switch between 'percentage increase', 'percentage of total' and 'percentage points'. A share rising from 20% to 25% is a rise of 5 **percentage points** but a **25%** increase.

cards.q: Sales rose from 40 to 60 units. The percentage increase is:
In a pie chart a category is 15% of the total. Its central angle is:
A share goes from 20% to 25%. Which statement is correct?
options: It rose by 5 percentage points (a 25% relative increase)
cards.explain: Percentage points measure the absolute change in a percentage.

notes.p:
The table below is **illustrative practice data** (laptop sales in thousand units):

Company A: 2021 — 40, 2022 — 50, 2023 — 60
Company B: 30, 36, 45
Company C: 50, 45, 54
Company D: 20, 25, 30

Yearly totals: 2021 = 140, 2022 = 156, 2023 = 189. Before answering, note the totals and the largest and smallest values — most questions reuse them.

**Q1. Percentage growth of A from 2021 to 2023?** (60 − 40)/40 = **50%**.

**Q2. Share of C in 2021?** 50/140 ≈ **35.7%**.

**Q3. In which year did C's sales fall?** 2022 (50 → 45, −10%).

**Q4. Average annual sales of B?** (30 + 36 + 45)/3 = **37** thousand.

**Q5. Angle for D in a 2023 pie chart?** 30/189 × 360 ≈ **57.1°**.

**Q6. Ratio of A's 2022 sales to D's 2022 sales?** 50 : 25 = **2 : 1**.

**Q7. Total market growth 2021 → 2023?** (189 − 140)/140 = **35%**.

`data = {'A': [40, 50, 60], 'B': [30, 36, 45], 'C': [50, 45, 54], 'D': [20, 25, 30]}
years = [2021, 2022, 2023]
totals = [sum(v[i] for v in data.values()) for i in range(3)]
print(totals)
print({k: round((v[2] - v[1]) / v[1] * 100, 1) for k, v in data.items()})

print(round((totals[2] - totals[0]) / totals[0] * 100, 1))
cagr = (data['A'][2] / data['A'][0]) ** 0.5 - 1

Output:
`[140, 156, 189]
{'A': 20.0, 'B': 25.0, 'C': 20.0, 'D': 20.0}
35.7 57.1
35.0
22.47 % compound annual growth for A`

A grew 50% in two years, which is about 22.47% per year compounded — not 25%, because growth compounds.

Some placement tests present DI as a caselet (a paragraph of numbers) instead of a chart: convert it into a small table first. For 'how many years/companies satisfy …' questions, mark each one with a tick to avoid double counting. If a chart has no total and the question asks for actual values, check whether the total is given elsewhere — without it only shares can be compared.
points: Steepest line segment = largest absolute change.
Doubling = +100%; halving = −50%.
Average of percentages ≠ percentage of totals.

notes.p:
**Q: Which company had the smallest share of the 2022 total?** A: D, 25/156 ≈ 16%.

**Q: By what percent did total sales grow from 2022 to 2023?** A: (189 − 156)/156 ≈ 21.2%.

**Q: What percentage of the three-year total of C was sold in 2023?** A: 54/149 ≈ 36.2%.

**Q: If A grows 20% again in 2024, its sales will be?** A: 60 × 1.2 = 72 thousand.
Remember:
points: % change on the old value.
Share = part/total; pie angle = share × 360°.
Percentage points vs percent.
Compound growth: (final/initial)^(1/n) − 1.
Write down totals first.
Approximate only when options are far apart.

cards.title: 2-D formulas
points: Rectangle: area lb, perimeter 2(l + b), diagonal √(l² + b²)
Triangle: ½ × base × height; Heron: √(s(s − a)(s − b)(s − c)), s = (a + b + c)/2
Equilateral triangle: (√3/4)a²
Circle: πr², circumference 2πr; sector: (θ/360) × πr²
Trapezium: ½ × (sum of parallel sides) × height

cards.title: 3-D formulas
points: Cube: volume a³, surface 6a², diagonal a√3
Cuboid: lbh, surface 2(lb + bh + hl), diagonal √(l² + b² + h²)
Cylinder: πr²h, curved 2πrh, total 2πr(r + h)
Cone: ⅓πr²h, slant l = √(r² + h²), curved πrl
Sphere: (4/3)πr³, surface 4πr²; hemisphere: (2/3)πr³, total 3πr²

cards.title: Geometry facts
cards.body: Angles in a triangle sum to 180°; exterior angle = sum of the two opposite interior angles. Sum of interior angles of an n-gon = (n − 2) × 180°; each exterior angle of a regular n-gon = 360°/n. Pythagorean triples: 3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17, 7-24-25. The angle in a semicircle is 90°.

cards.title: Scaling and percentage change
points: Lengths × k → areas × k², volumes × k³
Radius +10% → area +21%, volume +33.1%
Melting and recasting keeps volume constant
Similar triangles: ratio of areas = (ratio of sides)²

cards.title: Recasting
cards.body: A metal sphere of radius 6 cm is melted into a wire of radius 0.2 cm. Length: (4/3)π(6³) = π(0.2²)L → 288 = 0.04L → L = **7200 cm = 72 m**.

cards.q: If the radius of a circle increases by 20%, its area increases by:
Each interior angle of a regular hexagon is:
The volume of a cone is 1/3 of the volume of a cylinder with the same:
cards.explain: ⅓πr²h vs πr²h.

notes.p: Placement aptitude sections ask direct formula questions (area of a path around a garden, cost of painting walls, water flowing through a pipe), scaling questions (percentage change in area or volume), and recasting questions (one solid melted into others). Write the formula first, plug numbers last, and keep units consistent (1 m³ = 1000 litres; 1 hectare = 10,000 m²).

notes.h: Worked example 1: path around a garden
notes.p:
A rectangular garden 40 m × 30 m has a 2 m wide path all around it, outside. Path area = outer area − inner area = (44 × 34) − (40 × 30) = 1496 − 1200 = **296 m²**. At ₹50 per m², paving costs ₹14,800.
Shortcut: for a path of width w outside an l × b rectangle, area = 2w(l + b + 2w) = 2 × 2 × (40 + 30 + 4) = 296 ✓.

Water flows through a pipe of internal radius 7 cm at 5 m/s into a cylindrical tank of radius 1 m. How fast does the water level rise?
Flow per second = π(0.07)² × 5 m³. Tank cross-section = π(1)² m².
Rise per second = 0.0049 × 5 / 1 = 0.0245 m = **2.45 cm/s**. The π cancels — always look for that before multiplying out.

s = (13 + 14 + 15) / 2; print(math.sqrt(s * (s - 13) * (s - 14) * (s - 15)))
print(round(4 / 3 * 6 ** 3 / 0.2 ** 2))
print(round(1.1 ** 2 - 1, 3), round(1.1 ** 3 - 1, 3))
print(round(0.07 ** 2 * 5 / 1 ** 2 * 100, 2), 'cm/s')
print([(n - 2) * 180 / n for n in (5, 6, 8)])`

84.0
7200

[108.0, 120.0, 135.0]`

Every hand result above is confirmed, including the 21% and 33.1% growth for a 10% larger radius.

**Q: The diagonal of a square is 10√2 cm. Its area?** A: Side = 10 cm → 100 cm².

**Q: How many 2 cm cubes fit in a 10 cm cube?** A: (10/2)³ = 125.

**Q: A wheel of radius 35 cm makes 1000 revolutions. Distance covered (π = 22/7)?** A: 1000 × 2 × 22/7 × 35 cm = 220,000 cm = 2.2 km.

**Q: The two legs of a right triangle are 9 and 12. Hypotenuse?** A: 15 (a 3-4-5 triple scaled by 3).

**Q: A cylinder and a sphere have equal radius r and equal volume. Height of the cylinder?** A: πr²h = (4/3)πr³ → h = 4r/3.
Remember:
points: Write the formula, then substitute.
Heron for three known sides.
Areas scale by k², volumes by k³.
Recasting conserves volume.
Interior angle sum (n − 2) × 180°.
1 m³ = 1000 L; check units before answering.
Look for π to cancel.

cards.title: Number series checklist
points: Differences (and differences of differences)
Squares / cubes ± constant
×k ± c patterns
Two interleaved (alternate) series
Primes

cards.title: Letter positions
cards.body: Know A=1 … Z=26 instantly. Memory hook EJOTY = 5, 10, 15, 20, 25. Opposite letters add to 27: A↔Z, M↔N, D↔W.

cards.title: Coding-decoding
cards.body: Find the rule on the given word: fixed shift (+1, +2), reverse order, opposite letter, or position numbers. Then apply the same rule to the new word.

cards.title: Shift code
cards.body: MANGO → OCPIQ: each letter +2. So APPLE → CRRNG.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: If a series doesn't fit in 30 seconds, check alternate terms separately — TCS and Accenture love interleaved series.

cards.explain: Perfect squares: 6² = 36.

cards.q: If ROSE is coded TQUG, how is LILY coded?
cards.explain: Each letter +2: L→N, I→K, L→N, Y→A (wraps around).

cards.q: Find the odd one out: 3, 5, 9, 11
cards.explain: All others are prime; 9 = 3 × 3.

notes.h: How to attack a number series
notes.p:
Most series in IT placement tests follow a small set of patterns. Check them in this order and you will crack 90% of questions in under a minute: (1) **differences** between terms, (2) differences of differences, (3) **multiplication/division** pattern like ×2 + 1, (4) **squares and cubes** (n², n³, n² ± 1), (5) **primes**, (6) **two alternating series** hidden in one.

Write the differences under the terms. If the differences themselves form a pattern (2, 4, 6, 8 or 3, 9, 27), the next term follows quickly.

Memorise letter positions: A = 1, E = 5, J = 10, O = 15, T = 20, Y = 25 (the word **EJOTY** helps). The **opposite letter** of any letter sums to 27 with it: A ↔ Z, B ↔ Y, M ↔ N.

Example: B, E, H, K, ? jumps by +3 each time → **N**. Example: AZ, BY, CX, ? → **DW** (first letter moves forward, second is its opposite).

Coding questions hide a rule that changes a word letter by letter. Common rules: shift each letter by a fixed number, replace with the opposite letter, reverse the word, or shift by a changing amount (+1, +2, +3 …).

**Example 1 (shift):** COMPUTER is coded DPNQVUFS (each letter +1). Then KEYBOARD → **LFZCPBSE**.

**Example 2 (opposite letter):** CAT → XZG because C(3) ↔ X(24), A(1) ↔ Z(26), T(20) ↔ G(7).

**Example 3 (word-based):** if 'sky is blue' = 'ta na pa' and 'blue is nice' = 'pa ra na', the common words 'is' and 'blue' share codes 'na' and 'pa'. Compare more sentences to fix which is which.

Writing the rule as code is a great way to check your own decoding and to prepare for string questions in coding rounds:

`def shift(word, k):
    return "".join(chr((ord(c) - 65 + k) % 26 + 65) for c in word)

def opposite(word):
    return "".join(chr(155 - ord(c)) for c in word)  # 65 + 90 = 155

print(shift("KEYBOARD", 1))
print(opposite("CAT"))
seq = [3, 7, 15, 31, 63]
print(seq[-1] * 2 + 1)`

Output:
`LFZCPBSE
XZG
127`

**Q: Find the wrong term: 2, 5, 10, 17, 26, 38, 50.** A: Pattern n² + 1 gives 2, 5, 10, 17, 26, 37, 50 — so **38** is wrong.

**Q: If MOUSE is written as PRXVH, how is SHIFT written?** A: Each letter +3 → **VKLIW**.

**Q: In a code, 'DELHI' is 'EDMGJ'? Find the rule.** A: Letters alternate +1, −1, +1, −1, +1.
points: Trap: assuming a single series when terms alternate.
Trap: wrapping around the alphabet (Z + 1 = A).
Trap: 'wrong term' questions — check every term, not just the last.

notes.p: Remember:
points: Check differences first, then ratios, squares/cubes, primes, alternating.
Opposite letters add to 27.
Coding: shift, opposite, reverse or changing shift.
Write the positions under letters to see the jump.
Verify your rule on every letter before answering.

cards.title: Draw, don't imagine
cards.body: Draw a family tree: horizontal lines for siblings/spouses, vertical lines for generations, mark + for male and − for female. Never assume gender from a name.

cards.title: Classic statement
cards.body: Riya, pointing to a man: 'He is the son of my grandfather's only son.' Grandfather's only son = Riya's father. His son = Riya's brother.

cards.title: Coded relations
cards.body: Questions like 'A + B means A is the father of B, A × B means A is the sister of B' — decode one symbol at a time, left to right, and draw as you go.

cards.title: Directions
cards.body: North up, East right. Turning right from North → East; left from North → West. Use Pythagoras for the shortest distance from the start.

cards.title: Direction example
cards.body: Walk 3 km north, turn right, walk 4 km. You are 5 km (3-4-5 triangle) from the start, towards the north-east.

cards.title: Shadows
cards.body: Sun rises in the east, so in the morning shadows fall to the west; in the evening they fall to the east. At noon (in India) shadows are minimal.

cards.q: A man walks 6 km east, turns left and walks 8 km. How far is he from the start?
cards.explain: Left from east is north. √(6² + 8²) = 10 km.

cards.q: A is B's sister, C is B's mother and D is C's father. How is A related to D?
cards.explain: A is C's daughter; C is D's daughter → A is D's granddaughter.

cards.q: In the morning you stand facing the sun. Your shadow falls towards:
cards.explain: Facing the rising sun means facing east; the shadow is behind you, to the west.

notes.h: Blood relations: draw a family tree
notes.p:
Never solve blood relations in your head. Draw a **family tree**: generations go up and down, spouses are joined with a double line, and gender is marked with + (male) and − (female). Each statement adds one link.

Learn the vocabulary: father's or mother's brother = **uncle**; brother's or sister's son = **nephew**; son's wife = **daughter-in-law**; wife's brother = **brother-in-law**; father's father = **paternal grandfather**.

**Example 1.** Pointing to a man, Riya says, 'He is the son of my grandfather's only son.' Riya's grandfather's only son is Riya's father, and his son is **Riya's brother**.

**Example 2.** A is B's sister. C is B's mother. D is C's father. E is D's mother. How is A related to D? A and B are C's children; C is D's daughter; so A is **D's granddaughter**.

Some tests use symbols: 'A + B means A is the father of B, A − B means A is the wife of B, A × B means A is the brother of B'. Translate each symbol into a tree link one at a time from left to right. For 'P + Q × R', P is the father of Q, Q is the brother of R, so **P is the father of R**.

Watch for gender: a relation such as 'child' or 'sibling' does not tell gender. If the question cannot decide gender, the answer is often 'cannot be determined'.

Draw axes with **N up, E right**. Turning **right** = clockwise 90°; turning **left** = anticlockwise 90°. Track each move as a change in (x, y). The shortest distance from the start uses **Pythagoras**.

**Example 3.** A man walks 3 km north, turns right and walks 4 km, then turns right and walks 3 km. Net position: 4 km east, 0 km north, so he is **4 km east** of the start.

**Example 4.** Ravi walks 5 km east, turns left and walks 12 km. Distance from start = √(25 + 144) = **13 km**, towards north-east.

**Example 5 (angles).** Facing north, turn 90° clockwise, then 135° anticlockwise. Bearing 0 + 90 − 135 = −45 → 315°, so he faces **north-west**.

**Shadows:** in the morning the sun is in the east, so shadows fall to the **west**; in the evening shadows fall to the **east**.

`import math
dirs = {"N": (0, 1), "E": (1, 0), "S": (0, -1), "W": (-1, 0)}
order = "NESW"

def walk(moves, facing="N"):
    x = y = 0
    for turn, dist in moves:
        i = order.index(facing)
        facing = order[(i + {"R": 1, "L": -1, "S": 0}[turn]) % 4]
        dx, dy = dirs[facing]
        x, y = x + dx * dist, y + dy * dist
    return x, y, math.hypot(x, y)

print(walk([("S", 3), ("R", 4), ("R", 3)]))
print(walk([("S", 5), ("L", 12)], facing="E"))`

Output:
`(4, 0, 4.0)
(5, 12, 13.0)`

Here 'S' means go straight in the current facing direction.

**Q: Introducing a woman, Aman says, 'Her mother is the only daughter of my mother.' How is Aman related to the woman?** A: The only daughter of Aman's mother is Aman's sister, so Aman is the woman's **maternal uncle**.

**Q: A boy walks 10 m south, turns left 10 m, turns left 10 m. Which direction is he from the start?** A: East.
points: Trap: assuming gender from a name.
Trap: left/right when the person is facing south (left is east then).
Trap: confusing 'distance travelled' with 'distance from start'.

notes.p: Checklist:
points: Always draw a tree with + and − for gender.
Decode symbol relations left to right.
N up, E right; right turn = clockwise.
Use Pythagoras for straight-line distance.
Morning shadow → west; evening shadow → east.
'Cannot be determined' is a valid answer when gender is unknown.

cards.title: Syllogisms with Venn diagrams
cards.body: Draw the least-overlap diagram that satisfies every statement. A conclusion follows only if it is true in every possible diagram.

cards.title: Quick rules
points: All + All → All
All + No → No
Some + All → Some
Some + No → Some … not
Some + Some → no definite conclusion

cards.title: Either-or case
cards.body: When neither 'Some A are B' nor 'No A is B' follows individually but they cover all possibilities for the same pair, answer 'either I or II follows'.

cards.title: Example
cards.body: All cats are dogs; all dogs are birds. 'All cats are birds' follows. 'Some birds are cats' follows. 'All birds are cats' does not.

cards.title: Seating: linear & circular
cards.body: Place the definite clues first, then branch on the rest. Facing the centre of a circle, your left is clockwise; facing outward, it's reversed.

cards.title: Linear example
cards.body: Five people in a row face north. A is at the left end, C is in the middle, B is immediately right of C, E sits left of D. Row: A E C B D.

cards.q: Some pens are books. All books are tables. Which follows? I. Some pens are tables. II. All tables are pens.
cards.explain: Some + All gives 'Some pens are tables'. Nothing says all tables are pens.

cards.q: In the row A E C B D (left to right), who is second from the right?
cards.explain: From the right: D (1st), B (2nd).

cards.q: No cat is a rat. All rats are mice. Conclusion: 'Some mice are not cats.'
options: Only if all mice are rats
cards.explain: The mice that are rats are definitely not cats, so 'some mice are not cats' is always true.

notes.p:
A syllogism gives statements you must accept as true (even if they sound silly) and asks which conclusions **definitely** follow. Draw **Venn diagrams** and try to break each conclusion: if you can draw any valid diagram where the conclusion is false, it does **not follow**.

Four statement types: **All A are B**, **No A is B**, **Some A are B**, **Some A are not B**.
points: All + All → All (All A are B, All B are C → All A are C).
All + No → No (All A are B, No B is C → No A is C).
Some + All → Some (Some A are B, All B are C → Some A are C).
Some + No → Some not (Some A are B, No B is C → Some A are not C).
Two 'Some' statements → no definite conclusion.
'All A are B' also gives 'Some B are A' (conversion).

notes.p:
**Example 1.** Statements: All pens are books. Some books are tables. Conclusions: I. Some pens are tables. II. Some tables are books. Draw pens inside books; tables may overlap books outside the pens region. I does not follow; II follows by conversion. **Answer: only II.**

**Example 2 (either-or).** Statements: Some cats are dogs. Conclusions: I. All cats are dogs. II. Some cats are not dogs. Neither follows alone, but the two together cover all cases (either all cats are dogs or some are not). **Answer: either I or II.**

**Possibility questions:** 'All A being C is a possibility' is true if you can draw at least one diagram where it happens without breaking the statements.

**Linear, facing north:** your left is the viewer's left. **Facing south:** the person's left is the viewer's right. **Circular, facing the centre:** a person's **left is clockwise** and right is anticlockwise. Facing outward reverses this.

Method: draw the slots, place the **fixed** clues first (ends, middle, 'immediate'), then the conditional ones. When two cases appear, keep both and eliminate with later clues.

**Example 3.** Five friends P, Q, R, S, T sit in a row facing north. R is in the middle. P is at the left end. Q is immediately right of R. T is not next to P. Slots 1–5: P = 1, R = 3, Q = 4. T cannot be at 2 (next to P), so T = 5 and S = 2. **Order: P S R Q T.**

Coding a puzzle with permutations is a good habit for checking homework (and is a common interview question):

`from itertools import permutations
for row in permutations("PQRST"):
    pos = {p: i for i, p in enumerate(row)}
    if (pos["R"] == 2 and pos["P"] == 0 and pos["Q"] == pos["R"] + 1
            and abs(pos["T"] - pos["P"]) != 1):
        print("".join(row))`

Output:
`PSRQT`

**Q: Statements: No man is a tree. All trees are green. Conclusion: Some green things are not men.** A: Follows. Some green things are trees (conversion of All), and no tree is a man.

**Q: In a circle of 8 facing the centre, who sits third to the left of A?** A: Count three seats clockwise from A.
points: Trap: using real-world knowledge instead of the given statements.
Trap: 'Some A are B' does not mean 'Some A are not B'.
Trap: forgetting left/right flip when people face the centre or face outward.

notes.p: Remember:
points: Try to break each conclusion with a diagram.
All+All=All, All+No=No, Some+All=Some, Some+No=Some not.
Two particular statements give no definite conclusion.
Either-or: complementary pair about the same two terms.
Circle facing centre: left = clockwise.
Place fixed clues first; carry multiple cases until eliminated.

cards.title: Puzzle method
cards.body: Draw a **grid**: one row per person, one column per attribute (floor, day, colour, city). Fill **definite** clues first, then clues that restrict to two cases, and branch on those cases. Cross out impossibilities; one case usually dies quickly.

cards.title: Ranking formulas
points: Total = rank from top + rank from bottom − 1
Persons between two people = difference in their ranks − 1 (same direction)
If positions are swapped, use the change in one person's rank to find the other's

cards.title: Rank arithmetic
cards.body: Riya is 12th from the top and 19th from the bottom of a class. Total = 12 + 19 − 1 = **30** students.

cards.title: Data sufficiency format
cards.body: A question is followed by statements I and II. Decide whether the data is sufficient — not the actual answer. Standard options: (A) I alone; (B) II alone; (C) both together needed; (D) either alone; (E) neither, even together. Check I alone, then II alone, then together.

cards.title: DS example
cards.body: Q: Is x > y? I: x − y = 3. II: x + y = 10. I alone: x − y = 3 > 0 → yes, sufficient. II alone gives no comparison. Answer: **I alone** is sufficient (A). You never needed x and y themselves.

cards.title: Inequality chains
cards.body: From A > B ≥ C = D < E: A > C is definite; A vs E is unknown. A conclusion holds only if every link between the two letters points the same way. 'Either–or' applies when two conclusions are each uncertain but together cover all cases (e.g. A ≥ E or A < E).

cards.q: In a row, Amit is 7th from the left and 12th from the right. How many people are in the row?
Q: What is the value of n? I: n is a prime between 10 and 15. II: n is odd. Which is correct?
cards.explain: I allows 11 or 13; II does not narrow it to one value.

cards.q: Given P > Q = R ≥ S, which must be true?
cards.explain: P > Q = R ≥ S gives P > S; R and S may be equal.

notes.p: Puzzles come as sets of 3–5 questions on one arrangement, so solving the arrangement once earns several marks. Spend the first minute listing entities and attributes, then build the grid. Typical types: floor puzzles (who lives on which floor), scheduling (days of the week), box stacking, and comparison puzzles (who is taller or heavier).

Five people P, Q, R, S, T live on floors 1–5 (1 = bottom), one per floor.
Clues: (1) R lives on an even floor. (2) Q lives immediately above T. (3) P lives on the top floor. (4) S lives below R.
P = 5 (clue 3). R ∈ {2, 4}.
Case R = 2: S below → S = 1. Remaining floors 3, 4 for Q and T with Q directly above T → T = 3, Q = 4 ✓.
Case R = 4: Q and T need two consecutive floors among {1, 2, 3}, and S must be below R. Q–T = 3–2 leaves S = 1 ✓; Q–T = 2–1 leaves S = 3 ✓. Both work, so this case is not unique.
The clues as given leave **three** valid arrangements — a hint that a question will add another clue. With an extra clue 'T is not on an odd floor', only R = 4, T = 2, Q = 3, S = 1 survives. Always check uniqueness.

Never solve completely — stop as soon as you know whether a unique answer exists. For yes/no questions, a statement is sufficient if it gives a **definite yes or a definite no**. Watch for hidden constraints in the question (x is a positive integer, the shape is a square). If both statements give the same information, the answer cannot be 'both together'.
points: Combine only after each statement alone fails.
A definite 'no' is still sufficient.
Check whether integers, positives or distinct values are stated.

notes.p: Remember:
points: Grid + definite clues first + branch on two-case clues.
Total = top rank + bottom rank − 1.
DS: I alone, II alone, then together.
Sufficient = unique value or definite yes/no.
Inequality conclusions need same-direction links.
Check that a puzzle's answer is unique.

chapters.title: Critical reasoning: statements, assumptions, conclusions & arguments

cards.title: Assumption
cards.body: An **assumption** is an unstated belief the author must take for granted for the statement to make sense. Test: negate it — if the statement then collapses, it is an implicit assumption. Example: 'Use Brand X toothpaste for whiter teeth' assumes people want whiter teeth and that ads influence buying.

cards.title: Conclusion
cards.body: A **conclusion** must follow from the given statements alone, with no outside knowledge. Reject options that go beyond the text, use extreme words (always, only, all) without support, or merely restate a possibility as a certainty.

cards.title: Strong vs weak arguments
cards.body: A **strong** argument is directly related to the question, important, and backed by reasoning or facts. A **weak** one is emotional, trivial, ambiguous, or merely a slogan ('No, because it is our tradition'). Each argument is judged on its own.

cards.title: Courses of action
cards.body: A course of action is acceptable if it is **practical**, addresses the problem directly (or reduces its harm), and is within the authority of the one acting. Extreme steps (ban all vehicles, close every school) usually fail the practicality test.

cards.title: Cause and effect
cards.body: Decide whether one event caused the other, both have a common cause, or they are independent. The **cause** comes first and explains the effect; a government decision (cause) may lead to a price change (effect), but two effects of one cause are not cause and effect of each other.

cards.title: Strengthen and weaken
cards.body: In argument questions, first find the **conclusion** and the **evidence**. A strengthener supports the link between them; a weakener breaks the link (alternative cause, unrepresentative sample, correlation without causation). Ignore options about unrelated details.

cards.q: Statement: 'The city plans to add more buses to reduce traffic jams.' Which is an implicit assumption?
options: More buses will lead some people to stop using personal vehicles
Traffic jams happen only in winter
cards.explain: Without this belief, adding buses would not reduce jams.

cards.q: Should mobile phones be banned in schools? Argument: 'Yes, because many students use them to cheat in exams.' This argument is:
options: Strong only if all students cheat
cards.explain: It is relevant and gives a real, important reason.

cards.q: 'Sales of umbrellas rose sharply; there were heavy rains this month.' The rain is best described as:
options: The cause of higher umbrella sales
A common effect of a third cause
cards.explain: Heavy rain explains the increased demand and came first.

notes.p:
Critical-reasoning questions in placement tests are short paragraphs followed by 'which assumption is implicit', 'which conclusion follows', 'which argument is strong', or 'which course of action should be taken'. The skill is staying inside the text: use only what is written plus common sense, and avoid importing opinions or outside facts.

Read the question stem first so you know what you are hunting for, then read the statement once slowly. Underline the claim, the evidence and any qualifiers such as 'some', 'most', 'only' or 'likely', because these words usually decide which options survive.

**Statement:** 'Our company will launch an online course next month to train 10,000 students.'
Assumption I: There is demand for such a course. — If nobody wanted it, the launch plan would not make sense → **implicit**.
Assumption II: All 10,000 students will finish the course. — The plan needs enrolment, not completion → **not implicit**.
Assumption III: The company has or can build the platform by next month. — Negate it and the plan fails → **implicit**.
Answer: I and III.

notes.h: Worked example 2: conclusions and courses of action
notes.p:
**Statement:** 'In the last three months, 40% of the city's dengue cases were reported from areas with stagnant water near construction sites.'
Conclusion I: Stagnant water at construction sites contributes to dengue. — Reasonable inference from the data → **follows**.
Conclusion II: Construction should be banned in the city. — Extreme and not stated → **does not follow**.
Course of action: 'The municipal body should inspect construction sites and penalise those with stagnant water.' — Practical, targeted, within authority → **should be taken**. 'All residents should leave those areas.' → impractical → **not taken**.

**Question:** Should all government offices switch to a five-day working week?
Argument I: 'Yes, it will save electricity and fuel on the sixth day.' — Relevant, important, gives a reason → **strong**.
Argument II: 'No, employees will become lazy.' — An unsupported generalisation → **weak**.
Argument III: 'Yes, many private companies already do it.' — Imitation is not a reason by itself → **weak**.

**Weakening.** Claim: 'Students who attend coaching score higher, so coaching improves scores.' The strongest weakener points to another cause: 'Students who join coaching already had higher marks before joining.' This shows the data may reflect who joins coaching, not what coaching does — the classic correlation-versus-causation gap.
Avoid these mistakes:
points: Choosing a 'true in real life' option that the passage does not support.
Treating correlation as proof of causation.
Accepting extreme words without support.
Rejecting a reasonable assumption because it is not stated — assumptions are, by definition, unstated.
Judging two arguments together instead of separately.

notes.p: Remember:
points: Assumption: negate it — does the statement collapse?
Conclusion: must follow from the text alone.
Strong argument: relevant, important, reasoned.
Course of action: practical, direct, within authority.
Cause precedes and explains the effect.
Find conclusion and evidence before strengthen/weaken.

chapters.title: Analogy, classification & visual reasoning (dice, cubes, mirrors, figures)

cards.title: Analogy
cards.body: Find the exact relation in the first pair and apply it to the second. Common relations: worker–tool (carpenter : saw), part–whole (petal : flower), product–raw material (paper : pulp), degree (warm : hot), function (pen : write). Number analogies: squares, cubes, n² + 1, primes.

cards.title: Classification (odd one out)
cards.body: Three items share a property; one does not. Check category, function, letters (vowels, positions), and number properties (prime, square, divisible by). If two different rules each pick a different odd one, prefer the more specific, obvious rule.

cards.title: Dice
points: Standard die: opposite faces sum to 7 (1–6, 2–5, 3–4)
Two positions sharing one face: the other faces in the same rotational order are opposite
Faces adjacent to a common face can never be opposite to it
In a net, faces separated by one square in a straight line are opposite

cards.title: Mirror and water images
points: Mirror (vertical, on the right): left ↔ right swap; top and bottom stay
Water image: top ↔ bottom swap
Clock in a mirror: actual time = 11:60 − shown time (for times not at :00)
Letters symmetric about a vertical axis (A, H, I, M, O, T, U, V, W, X, Y) look the same in a mirror

cards.title: Mirror clock
cards.body: A clock seen in a mirror shows 4:20. Actual time = 11:60 − 4:20 = **7:40**. (For whole hours use 12:00 − time: a mirror showing 3:00 means 9:00.)

cards.title: Counting figures
cards.body: Triangles in a triangle divided by lines from one vertex to n points on the opposite side: (n + 1)(n + 2)/2. Squares in an n × n grid: n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6. Rectangles: [n(n + 1)/2]². Count systematically by size, never by eye.

cards.q: Doctor : Hospital :: Teacher : ?
cards.explain: Workplace relation.

cards.q: Find the odd one: 9, 25, 49, 81, 121, 143
cards.explain: All others are squares of odd numbers; 143 = 11 × 13.

cards.q: A clock seen in a mirror shows 2:30. The actual time is:

notes.p: Analogy, odd-one-out and visual items are quick marks in most aptitude sections. They reward a checklist approach: list possible relations or properties and test each, instead of waiting for inspiration. Visual questions (dice, cubes, mirror images, counting figures) follow fixed rules — once learnt, they are almost mechanical.

notes.h: Worked example 1: dice from two positions
notes.p:
Two views of the same die (not necessarily a standard one). View 1 shows 6 on top, 2 in front and 3 on the right. View 2 shows 6 on top, 4 in front and 2 on the right.
Faces 6 and 2 appear in both views, so they share an edge. Exactly two faces touch both 6 and 2 — the two faces at the ends of that edge — and those two faces are opposite each other. Here they are 3 and 4, so **3 is opposite 4**.
The remaining faces 1 and 5 must be opposite 6 and 2 in some order; two views alone cannot decide which, so questions add a third view.
Rules worth memorising: faces seen together in one view are never opposite; with two common faces, the uncommon faces are opposite; on a standard die opposite faces sum to 7.

`from itertools import combinations
def squares(n): return sum((n - k + 1) ** 2 for k in range(1, n + 1))
def rectangles(n): return len(list(combinations(range(n + 1), 2))) ** 2
def triangles_from_vertex(points): return (points + 1) * (points + 2) // 2
print([squares(n) for n in range(1, 6)], rectangles(4), triangles_from_vertex(3))
def mirror_time(h, m):
    t = (11 * 60 + 60) - (h * 60 + m)
    t %= 720
    return (t // 60 or 12, t % 60)
print(mirror_time(4, 20), mirror_time(2, 30), mirror_time(3, 0))`

Output:
`[1, 5, 14, 30, 55] 100 10
(7, 40) (9, 30) (9, 0)`

A 4 × 4 grid holds 30 squares and 100 rectangles; a triangle with 3 points on its base joined to the apex holds 10 triangles. The mirror-clock helper confirms 4:20 → 7:40, 2:30 → 9:30 and 3:00 → 9:00.

**Letters:** BD, FH, JL, NQ — the first three skip one letter (B_D), NQ skips two → **NQ** is odd.
**Words:** Mercury, Venus, Moon, Mars — the Moon is a satellite, the rest are planets.
**Numbers:** 3 : 27 :: 5 : ? → cube → **125**. 2 : 5 :: 4 : ? → n² + 1 → **17**.
**Pairs:** choose the pair with the same relation as 'Author : Book' → 'Composer : Symphony' (creator : creation).
Remember:
points: State the exact relation before choosing.
Odd one out: category, function, letters, number property.
Dice: opposite faces of a standard die sum to 7; faces seen together are not opposite.
Mirror swaps left–right; water swaps top–bottom.
Mirror clock: 11:60 − time.
Squares in n × n grid: n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6; rectangles [n(n + 1)/2]².

cards.title: Subject–verb agreement
points: Each / every / either / neither + singular verb: 'Each of the students has…'
Neither…nor / either…or: verb agrees with the nearer subject
Collective noun as one unit takes singular: 'The team is…'
'One of the + plural noun': one of the best players

cards.title: Articles
cards.body: Use 'an' before a vowel sound (an hour, an MBA), 'a' before a consonant sound (a university, a one-rupee coin). 'The' for something specific or unique.

cards.title: Tenses: since vs for
cards.body: 'Since' + point of time (since 2019); 'for' + period (for five years). Use present perfect continuous: 'I have been working here since 2022.'

cards.title: Common errors
points: discuss about → discuss
return back → return
cope up with → cope with
revert back → reply
more better → better

cards.title: Fix it
cards.body: 'The list of items are on the desk.' The subject is 'list' (singular) → 'The list of items is on the desk.'

cards.title: Error-spotting routine
cards.body: Check in order: subject–verb agreement, tense consistency, pronoun reference, preposition, parallelism ('to read, to write and to speak').

cards.q: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Neither the manager nor the employees was present.
Neither the manager nor the employees were present.
Neither the manager nor the employees is present.
Neither the manager or the employees were present.
cards.explain: With neither…nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject 'employees' (plural); 'neither' pairs with 'nor'.

cards.q: Spot the error: 'He is / one of the best player / in the team. / No error'
cards.explain: 'One of the' takes a plural noun: players.

cards.q: She has been living here ___ 2019.
cards.explain: 2019 is a point of time, so 'since'.

notes.p:
Placement English sections (TCS, Infosys, Accenture, Capgemini etc.) test grammar through **spot the error**, **sentence improvement** and **fill in the blanks**. You do not need fancy vocabulary; you need a short checklist of rules applied carefully.

Read the full sentence once for meaning, then scan in this order: **subject–verb agreement → tense → pronoun → article → preposition → modifier/parallelism**.

**Subject–verb agreement:** the verb agrees with the real subject, not the nearest noun. Wrong: 'The list of items are on the desk.' Right: 'The list of items **is** on the desk.' Words like each, every, either, neither, everyone take a **singular** verb.

**Tense consistency:** 'I have seen him yesterday' is wrong because a definite past time needs simple past: 'I **saw** him yesterday.' 'Since' with a point of time needs present perfect: 'I **have lived** here since 2020.'

**Articles:** use 'an' before a vowel **sound**: an hour, an MBA, a university, a one-rupee coin.

**Prepositions:** good **at** coding, interested **in**, married **to**, discuss (no 'about'), comprise (no 'of').

**Parallelism:** 'She likes reading, writing and **to swim**' → 'reading, writing and **swimming**'.

**1.** 'Neither the manager nor the engineers **was** present.' With neither…nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject (engineers), so the correct verb is **were**.

**2.** 'One of my friend **are** a developer.' Two errors: 'one of' takes a plural noun and singular verb → 'One of my **friends is** a developer.'

**3.** 'He is senior **than** me.' Latin comparatives (senior, junior, superior, prior) take **to**: 'senior to me'.

**4.** 'If I **was** you, I would accept the offer.' Imaginary condition uses **were**: 'If I were you'.

**5.** 'Hardly had I reached the station **than** the train left.' Hardly/scarcely pairs with **when**.

notes.h: Common errors in placement answers and emails
notes.p: Recruiters also judge your written English in essays and emails. Avoid these frequent Indian-English slips:
points: 'Revert back' → just 'reply' (revert already means return).
'Do the needful' → say exactly what you want done.
'I am having two years of experience' → 'I have two years of experience'.
'Discuss about' → 'discuss'.
'Myself Rahul' → 'I am Rahul' or 'My name is Rahul'.
'Kindly find the attached' → 'Please find attached'.

notes.p:
Do not change a sentence that is already correct; 'No error' is a real option and is right in roughly one out of five questions.

Collective nouns (team, jury, committee) usually take singular verbs when acting as one unit.

'The number of' takes singular; 'a number of' takes plural.
Grammar checklist:
points: Find the real subject before checking the verb.
Each/every/either/neither → singular verb.
Neither…nor / either…or → verb matches the nearer subject.
Definite past time → simple past, not present perfect.
'An' before vowel sounds (an hour, a university).
Senior/junior/prior take 'to'; hardly…when; no sooner…than.
Keep lists parallel.

cards.title: RC approach
cards.body: Skim the passage for its main idea and tone (1 minute), then read each question and go back to the exact lines. For fact questions, scanning beats rereading.

cards.title: RC question types
points: Main idea / best title
Inference: must be supported by the text
Tone: critical, neutral, optimistic…
Word meaning in context

cards.title: Elimination
cards.body: Reject options with extreme words (always, never, only) unless the passage says so, and options that are true in real life but not stated in the passage.

cards.title: Para-jumbles
cards.body: Find the opener: a sentence that introduces the topic without pronouns or connectors. Then link pairs: 'this', 'however', 'therefore' point back to a previous sentence.

cards.title: Vocabulary via roots
points: bene = good (benevolent), mal = bad (malevolent)
chron = time (chronic), ephem = short-lived
loqu = speak (eloquent), ambi = both (ambiguous)

cards.title: Opener test
cards.body: 'Cloud computing lets firms rent servers on demand.' can open a paragraph. 'However, costs rose.' cannot — 'however' needs something before it.

cards.q: Synonym of 'Ephemeral':
cards.explain: Ephemeral means lasting a very short time.

cards.q: Antonym of 'Benevolent':
cards.explain: Benevolent = well-meaning; malevolent = wishing harm.

cards.q: Which sentence most likely opens a paragraph?
options: Cloud computing lets companies rent servers on demand.
cards.explain: The others begin with connectors or pronouns that refer back to an earlier sentence.

notes.p:
RC passages in IT tests are 200–400 words on technology, business or social topics, with 3–5 questions. A reliable method: **read the questions first** (not the options), then read the passage once at a steady pace, marking the main idea of each paragraph in your head.

Question types: **main idea / title**, **specific detail**, **inference** (what the author would agree with), **tone** (critical, neutral, optimistic), and **vocabulary in context**.

For inference questions, pick the option that is **supported by the passage** and is the least extreme. Words like 'always', 'never', 'all' are usually wrong.

Look for the **opening sentence**: it introduces a topic and does not start with 'This', 'However', 'He' or 'Therefore'. Then link pairs using **pronouns** (it, they, this), **connectors** (however, therefore, also) and **time order**.

**Worked example.** P: However, most of them never get past the first page. Q: Every year, millions of people buy books on personal finance. R: The few who do finish often report real changes in how they spend. S: This is not because the books are dull, but because habits are hard to change.

Q introduces the topic, so it opens. P's 'However … them' refers to the buyers in Q. S explains P ('This is not because…'). R talks about 'the few who do finish', contrasting with P. **Order: Q P S R.**

Learn words in families using **roots**: 'bene' = good (benefit, benevolent), 'mal' = bad (malfunction, malicious), 'chron' = time (chronic, synchronise), 'scrib/script' = write (describe, manuscript).
