Placement-level synonym/antonym pairs to know: **abundant** – plentiful / scarce; **candid** – frank / evasive; **diligent** – hard-working / lazy; **obsolete** – outdated / modern; **ambiguous** – unclear / explicit; **mitigate** – reduce / worsen; **lucid** – clear / confusing.

For fill-in-the-blank, read the full sentence and predict the meaning before seeing options. Check contrast words: 'although' and 'but' signal an opposite idea.

notes.h: Common test questions with model answers
notes.p:
**Q: Choose the word closest in meaning to 'pragmatic'.** A: Practical.

**Q: Antonym of 'verbose'.** A: Concise.

**Q: 'Despite his ____ efforts, the project failed.' (a) half-hearted (b) relentless (c) lazy (d) careless.** A: (b) relentless — 'despite' needs a positive word that contrasts with failure.

**Q: Which title suits a passage on how remote work changes office culture?** A: The option that names both remote work and culture, not an option about one narrow detail.
These mistakes cost the most marks in verbal sections:
points: Choosing an option that is true in real life but not stated in the passage.
Picking an option that copies passage words but twists their meaning.
In para-jumbles, starting with a sentence that has an unexplained pronoun.
Spending more than 6–7 minutes on one passage; move on and return.

notes.p: Remember:
points: Read questions first, passage second.
Inference = supported and moderate, not extreme.
Para-jumble: find the opener, then link pronouns and connectors.
Learn words by roots and in pairs (synonym + antonym).
Use contrast words to guess blanks.
Manage time: about 1 minute per RC question.

cards.title: Structure
points: Subject: specific and short (e.g. 'Request for leave on 12–13 March')
Salutation: Dear Mr Sharma / Dear Hiring Team / Hello Priya
Body: purpose in the first line, details, clear request or next step
Closing: Regards / Best regards / Sincerely + full name, role, contact

cards.title: Tone
cards.body: Polite, direct and formal. Avoid SMS language (u, pls, thx), slang, ALL CAPS and excessive exclamation marks. One idea per paragraph, short sentences. Be specific about dates, times and what you need.

cards.title: Placement email tasks
cards.body: Some written-communication rounds give a situation, a set of **phrases to use**, and a word range. Use every given phrase (you may change its form only if allowed), stay within the word count, and keep to the facts given. Read the instructions for that test — formats differ by company and year.

cards.title: Useful phrases
points: Opening: I am writing to request / inform / follow up on …
Request: Could you please …; I would be grateful if …
Apology: I apologise for the inconvenience caused by …
Closing: Please let me know if you need any further information.
Follow-up: I wanted to follow up on my email dated …

cards.title: Common mistakes
cards.body: Vague subject lines ('Hi', 'Urgent'), missing attachments that the body mentions, wrong names, long unstructured paragraphs, replying-all unnecessarily, and ending without a clear request. Proofread names, dates and numbers last.

cards.title: Check before sending
cards.body: Who is the reader? What do I want them to do? Is that in the first two lines? Are the subject, attachments and recipients right? Would I be comfortable if this were forwarded to my manager?

cards.q: Which is the best subject line for asking HR to change your joining date?
options: Request to reschedule joining date from 1 July to 15 July
cards.explain: Specific and actionable.

cards.q: Which closing is appropriate for a formal email to a recruiter?
cards.explain: Polite, formal, with the full name.

cards.q: The first line of a professional email should usually:
options: State the purpose of the email
cards.explain: Readers decide from the first line whether to act now.

notes.p: At work most communication is written. Recruiters read your emails as a sample of your communication skills, and some aptitude tests include a written-English or email task scored on grammar, structure, use of given phrases and relevance. A clear email gets a faster, better reply.

**Situation:** you need two days' leave for a family function.

`Subject: Leave request for 12–13 March

Dear Ms Iyer,

I am writing to request leave on 12 and 13 March to attend a family function in Jaipur.

I have completed the testing tasks assigned for this sprint, and Rahul has agreed to handle any urgent issues on my module during these two days. I will be reachable on phone for anything critical.

Could you please approve the request? Please let me know if you need any further information.

Best regards,
Arjun Mehta
Software Engineer Trainee | +91 98xxxxxx10`

The purpose is in the first line, the handover answers the manager's main worry, and the request is explicit.

**Task:** write to the hotel manager about a booking problem using the phrases: *booked a room, not available, refund, earliest convenience* (about 100 words).

`Subject: Refund for unavailable room – booking ID 45821

Dear Hotel Manager,

I booked a room at your hotel for 5–7 May through your website (booking ID 45821). On arrival, I was told the room was not available, and I had to find another hotel late at night.

Since the payment of ₹6,400 was made in advance, I request a full refund to the original payment method. I have attached the booking confirmation and payment receipt.

Kindly process the refund at your earliest convenience and confirm by email.

Sincerely,
Neha Kapoor`

Every phrase is used naturally, the facts are specific, and the request is clear.

If there is no reply in a reasonable time, send a short follow-up in the same thread: 'I wanted to follow up on my email of 3 June regarding …'. When replying to an interview invitation, confirm the date, time and mode, and thank them. Decline politely with a reason when you cannot attend, and suggest alternatives.
points: Keep CC to people who need to know; use BCC for large lists.
Name attachments clearly (Resume_Ananya_Rao.pdf).
Use a professional email address, ideally firstname.lastname.

notes.h: Applying for a job by email
notes.p: Keep the body short — the resume carries the details. Mention the role and where you saw it in the first line, two or three lines on why you fit (skills, a project, a result), and a polite close. Example opening: 'I am writing to apply for the Graduate Engineer Trainee role advertised on your careers page.' Attach the resume as a PDF with a clear file name, and paste nothing confidential from previous employers or college portals. Send a brief thank-you email within a day after an interview.
Remember:
points: Specific subject line.
Purpose in the first line.
One idea per paragraph; short sentences.
Clear request or next step.
Formal closing with full name and contact.
Use all given phrases within the word limit.
Proofread names, dates, numbers and attachments.

cards.title: Data types (typical 64-bit compiler)
points: char 1 byte, int 4, float 4, double 8
sizeof is an operator, not a function
Integer overflow of signed int is undefined behaviour

cards.title: Integer division and %
cards.body: 7 / 2 = 3 and 7 % 2 = 1. Since C99, division truncates towards zero: −7 / 2 = −3 and −7 % 2 = −1. Watch for int/int when you expect a decimal.

cards.title: Pre vs post increment
cards.body:
int a = 5;
int b = a++;  // b = 5, a = 6
int c = ++a;  // a = 7, c = 7
Never use a++ twice in one expression (e.g. a++ + ++a) — it is undefined behaviour.

cards.title: Pointers
cards.body: int x = 10; int *p = &x; *p = 20; → x is now 20. Arrays decay to pointers: arr[i] is the same as *(arr + i).

cards.title: static local variable
switch fall-through
cards.body: Without break, execution continues into the next case. case 1: printf("A"); case 2: printf("B"); with input 1 prints AB.

cards.q: int a = 5; int b = a++ * 2; printf("%d %d", a, b); prints:
cards.explain: b uses the old value 5 → 10; then a becomes 6.

cards.q: printf("%d", 17 % 5); prints:
A function with static int c = 0; c++; printf("%d ", c); is called three times. Output:
cards.explain: The static variable is initialised once and retains its value.

notes.p:
Service companies love **'what is the output?'** questions in C because they test whether you understand how a computer really evaluates expressions. Most traps come from five areas: **integer division and modulo**, **pre/post increment**, **implicit type conversion**, **switch fall-through** and **pointers/arrays**.

Key facts: `int` division truncates toward zero, so `7/2` is 3 and `-7/2` is -3. The sign of `%` follows the dividend, so `-7 % 2` is -1. A `char` is a small integer, so `'A' + 2` is 67, which prints as `C` with `%c`.

notes.h: Pointers, arrays and memory in one page
notes.p:
A **pointer** stores an address. `*p` reads the value at that address; `&x` gives the address of `x`. An array name **decays** to a pointer to its first element, so `arr[i]` is the same as `*(arr + i)`. Inside a function, `sizeof` of an array parameter gives the pointer size, not the array size.

`malloc(n)` returns uninitialised memory; `calloc(count, size)` returns zero-filled memory; always `free()` what you allocate. A **dangling pointer** points to memory that was freed; a **memory leak** is allocated memory you can no longer free. Use `NULL` after `free` to avoid using a stale pointer.

**Q: Difference between `++i` and `i++`?** A: Both add 1. `++i` gives the new value; `i++` gives the old value then increments.

**Q: What is undefined behaviour? Give an example.** A: Code whose result the C standard does not define, so compilers may print anything. Example: `i = i++ + ++i;` modifies `i` twice without a sequence point.

**Q: Call by value vs call by reference in C?** A: C always passes by value; to let a function change a variable you pass its address (a pointer).

**Q: struct vs union?** A: A struct gives every member its own memory (size ≥ sum of members, plus padding). A union shares one block among members (size = largest member, plus padding).

**Q: What does `static` mean for a global variable?** A: It limits the variable's visibility to that source file.
Check these before choosing an option:
points: `printf("%d", 3.5)` with a float argument is undefined, not 3.
`if (x = 5)` assigns, so it is always true; you meant `==`.
A semicolon after `for(...);` makes an empty loop body.
Comparing signed and unsigned: `-1 < 1u` is false because -1 becomes a huge unsigned value.
Octal literals: `010` is 8, not 10.

notes.p: Five-minute recap:
points: Integer division truncates toward zero; `%` takes the dividend's sign.
`i++` returns old value, `++i` returns new value.
Missing `break` in switch → fall-through.
`static` local keeps value across calls.
`arr[i]` == `*(arr + i)`; arrays decay to pointers.
malloc = uninitialised, calloc = zeroed, always free.
Avoid modifying a variable twice in one expression.

cards.title: Java in one card
cards.body: Source compiles to bytecode that runs on the JVM, so the same .class runs anywhere ('write once, run anywhere'). Entry point: public static void main(String[] args).

cards.title: Java strings
cards.body: Strings are immutable. == compares references; .equals() compares content. Literals are interned in the string pool.

cards.title: == vs equals
Python numbers
cards.body: / is true division (7/2 = 3.5); // is floor division (7//2 = 3, −7//2 = −4). % takes the sign of the divisor: −7 % 3 = 2.

cards.title: Python slicing
cards.body: s[start:stop:step], stop excluded. s[1:4] → indices 1–3; s[::-1] reverses; s[-1] is the last element.

cards.title: Mutable default argument
cards.body:
def f(x, l=[]):
    l.append(x)
    return l
f(1) → [1]; f(2) → [1, 2]! The default list is created once. Use l=None and create a new list inside.

cards.q: print(-7 // 2) in Python outputs:
cards.explain: // floors towards negative infinity: −3.5 → −4.

cards.q: Java: String s1 = "abc"; String s2 = "abc"; s1 == s2 is:
cards.explain: Both literals refer to the same object in the string pool.

cards.q: Python: print("placement"[2:5])
cards.explain: Indices 2, 3, 4 → a, c, e.

notes.p:
Java code runs on the **JVM**: `javac` compiles `.java` into **bytecode** (`.class`), and the JVM runs it on any OS. The entry point is `public static void main(String[] args)`. Primitive types: byte (1 byte), short (2), int (4), long (8), float (4), double (8), char (2, Unicode), boolean.

**Strings are immutable.** String literals are stored in the **string pool**, so two equal literals share one object. `==` compares **references**; `.equals()` compares **content**. Wrapper classes like `Integer` cache values from **-128 to 127** by default, which creates a famous trap.

String concatenation is evaluated left to right: `1 + 2 + "3"` is "33", but `"3" + 1 + 2` is "312".

Python is **dynamically typed** and **interpreted** (compiled to bytecode internally). Everything is an object. **Lists** are mutable; **tuples** and **strings** are immutable. `==` compares values; `is` compares identity.

`/` always returns a float, `//` is **floor division** (rounds toward minus infinity), and `%` takes the sign of the divisor. Default arguments are evaluated **once**, so a mutable default like `[]` is shared across calls.

`def add(item, bucket=[]):
    bucket.append(item)
    return bucket

print(add(1)); print(add(2))
a = [1, 2, 3]; b = a; b.append(4); print(a)
print(7 // 2, -7 // 2, 7 % 3, -7 % 3)
s = "abcdef"; print(s[::-1], s[1:4])
print([x * x for x in range(5) if x % 2 == 0])
print(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3, round(0.1 + 0.2, 2) == 0.3)`

Output:
`[1]
[1, 2]
[1, 2, 3, 4]
3 -4 1 2
fedcba bcd
[0, 4, 16]
False True`

**Q: Why is Java called platform independent?** A: Source compiles to bytecode that any JVM can run; the JVM itself is platform-specific.

**Q: JDK vs JRE vs JVM?** A: JVM runs bytecode; JRE = JVM + libraries to run programs; JDK = JRE + compiler and tools to develop.

**Q: Why are Strings immutable in Java?** A: Safety for the string pool, thread safety, and secure use as keys and in class loading.

**Q: List vs tuple in Python?** A: List is mutable and uses []; tuple is immutable, uses (), and can be a dict key.

**Q: What is a Python decorator?** A: A function that takes a function and returns a new function, used with `@name` to add behaviour like logging.

**Q: Shallow vs deep copy?** A: Shallow copy copies the outer container but shares inner objects; `copy.deepcopy` copies everything recursively.
Commonly missed points:
points: Java: `==` on objects compares references.
Java: integer overflow wraps silently (`Integer.MAX_VALUE + 1` is negative).
Python: mutable default arguments persist.
Python: `b = a` does not copy a list.
Python: `-7 // 2` is -4, not -3.

notes.p: Remember:
points: Java: javac → bytecode → JVM.
`==` vs `.equals()`; Integer cache -128 to 127.
String concatenation is left to right.
Python: list mutable, tuple immutable.
`/` float, `//` floor, `%` follows divisor sign.
Never use a mutable default argument; use `None`.

cards.title: Class and object
cards.body: A class is a blueprint (fields + methods); an object is an instance created from it. Each object has its own state.

cards.title: Encapsulation
cards.body: Bundle data with the methods that use it and hide the data: private fields, public getters/setters that can validate input.

cards.title: Inheritance
cards.body: 'Is-a' reuse: class Dog extends Animal. Java allows single class inheritance (multiple via interfaces); C++ and Python allow multiple inheritance.

cards.title: Polymorphism
points: Compile-time: method overloading — same name, different parameters
Run-time: method overriding — subclass redefines a parent method; chosen by the actual object type

cards.title: Dynamic dispatch
Abstraction
cards.body: Expose what an object does, hide how. Achieved with abstract classes and interfaces. Example: List interface vs ArrayList/LinkedList implementations.

cards.q: Method overloading is an example of:
cards.explain: The compiler picks the overload from the argument types.

cards.q: Making fields private and exposing getters/setters is called:
cards.explain: Data hiding is encapsulation.

cards.q: Animal a = new Dog(); a.sound(); — if Dog overrides sound(), which runs?
cards.explain: Overridden methods are dispatched on the runtime object type.

notes.h: The four pillars in plain words
notes.p:
**Object-oriented programming (OOP)** organises code around **objects** that bundle data (fields) and behaviour (methods). A **class** is the blueprint; an **object** is one instance built from it.

**Encapsulation:** keep data private and expose safe methods (a bank account allows deposit, not direct balance edits). **Abstraction:** show what an object does and hide how (you call `area()` without knowing the formula). **Inheritance:** a child class reuses and extends a parent (Circle **is a** Shape). **Polymorphism:** one interface, many forms — a `Shape` reference can call the right `area()` for a Circle or a Rectangle.

Two kinds of polymorphism: **compile-time** (method **overloading** — same name, different parameters) and **runtime** (method **overriding** — child redefines a parent method, chosen by the actual object type at runtime).

notes.h: Abstract class vs interface, and other key terms
notes.p:
An **abstract class** can have fields, constructors and both abstract and concrete methods; a class can extend only one. An **interface** describes a capability (`Comparable`, `Runnable`); a class can implement many. Since Java 8 interfaces can have `default` and `static` methods.

**Constructor:** special method that initialises an object; it has no return type. **`this`** refers to the current object; **`super`** to the parent. **Composition** ('has a', a Car has an Engine) is often preferred over inheritance because it is more flexible.

**Q: Can we override a static method?** A: No. Static methods are hidden, not overridden, because they belong to the class.

**Q: Why does Java not support multiple inheritance of classes?** A: To avoid the diamond problem (ambiguity when two parents define the same method). Interfaces solve the need.

**Q: Overloading vs overriding?** A: Overloading: same name, different parameters, same class, decided at compile time. Overriding: same signature in child class, decided at runtime.

**Q: What is a final class?** A: A class that cannot be extended, e.g. `String`.

**Q: Give a real-life example of abstraction.** A: Driving a car with a steering wheel and pedals without knowing the engine internals.
Watch for:
points: Changing only the return type is not overloading (compile error).
Private methods are not inherited, so they cannot be overridden.
A parent reference cannot call child-only methods without a cast.
Constructors are not inherited, but the parent constructor runs first.

notes.p: Summary:
points: Class = blueprint, object = instance.
Encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, polymorphism.
Overloading = compile time; overriding = runtime.
Abstract class: single extend; interface: many implements.
Prefer composition ('has a') when 'is a' is unclear.
Use private fields + validated methods.

cards.title: Trace with a table
cards.body: Make one column per variable and one row per loop iteration. Update in the exact order written. Most pseudo-code MCQs (Capgemini, Accenture, Infosys) are won here.

cards.title: Operators you must know
points: a mod b = remainder; a / b on integers = floor in most pseudo-code
&& and || short-circuit

cards.title: Loop trace
cards.body:
sum = 0
for i = 1 to 5
  if i mod 2 == 0
    sum = sum + i
print sum
→ i = 2 and 4 are added → 6

cards.title: Recursion trace
Digit loop
cards.body:
rev = 0
while n > 0
  rev = rev * 10 + n mod 10
  n = n / 10
For n = 1234 → rev = 4321. Recognise this pattern instantly.

cards.title: Traps
cards.body: Off-by-one loop bounds ('to' inclusive?), integer division, variables updated inside the loop condition, and a recursive call before vs after the print.

cards.q:
a = 10, b = 3
a = a ^ b
b = a ^ b
a = a ^ b
print a, b

x = 1
for i = 1 to 4
  x = x * 2 + 1
print x

cards.explain: Digit sum: 4 + 7 + 2 = 13.

notes.p:
Pseudo-code questions (Capgemini, Accenture, TCS, Cognizant) give a short program in a C-like made-up language and ask for its output. The winning technique is a **trace table**: one column per variable, one row per step. Never try to hold more than two variables in your head.

Know the operators: `mod` or `%` is remainder; `&` (AND), `|` (OR), `^` (XOR) work on binary bits; `<<` multiplies by 2 per shift; `>>` divides by 2 per shift (for non-negative numbers). Integer division drops the fraction.

Pseudo-code: `a = 5, b = 3; for i = 1 to 3: a = a + b; b = a - b; end; print a, b`.

Trace: start (5, 3) → i = 1: a = 8, b = 5 → i = 2: a = 13, b = 8 → i = 3: a = 21, b = 13. Output **21 13**. Notice these are Fibonacci numbers — recognising patterns saves time.

notes.h: Worked examples 2–5 and a Python check
notes.p:
**Bitwise:** 5 = 101, 3 = 011. `5 & 3` = 001 = 1; `5 | 3` = 111 = 7; `5 ^ 3` = 110 = 6; `5 << 2` = 20; `5 >> 1` = 2.

**Recursion:** `fun(n): if n <= 1 return 1 else return n + fun(n - 2)`. `fun(7)` = 7 + 5 + 3 + 1 = **16**.

**Nested loop count:** `for i = 1 to 5: for j = 1 to i: count++` runs 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 = **15** times.

**Digit sum:** `while n > 0: s = s + n mod 10; n = n / 10` with n = 1234 gives **10**.

You can translate the pseudo-code into Python to confirm your traces while practising:

`a, b = 5, 3
for i in range(1, 4):
    a = a + b
    b = a - b
print(a, b)
print(5 & 3, 5 | 3, 5 ^ 3, 5 << 2, 5 >> 1)

def fun(n):
    return 1 if n <= 1 else n + fun(n - 2)
print(fun(7))

count = sum(1 for i in range(1, 6) for j in range(1, i + 1))
n, s = 1234, 0
while n > 0:
    s += n % 10
    n //= 10
print(count, s)`

Output:
`21 13
1 7 6 20 2
16
15 10`

notes.h: Common question types with short answers
notes.p:
**Q: How many times does `while (n > 1) n = n / 2` run for n = 64?** A: 64 → 32 → 16 → 8 → 4 → 2 → 1, so 6 times (log₂ 64).

**Q: What is s after `s = 0; for i = 1 to 10: if i mod 3 == 0 then s = s + i`?** A: 3 + 6 + 9 = 18.

**Q: Value of `17 mod 5 + 17 / 5` (integer)?** A: 2 + 3 = 5.

**Q: What does a loop `for i = 1 to n step 2` count?** A: ⌈n/2⌉ iterations.
Most errors come from:
points: Off-by-one: does 'to n' include n? Usually yes in pseudo-code.
Integer vs real division.
Variables updated in place (a changes before b uses it).
Global vs local variables with the same name.
Recursion base case reached earlier than you think.

notes.p: Remember:
points: Make a trace table; one row per step.
AND, OR, XOR on binary; << doubles, >> halves.
Count loop iterations with formulas (n(n+1)/2, log₂ n).
Watch updated values inside the same iteration.
Recursion: write calls as a stack, then unwind.
Spot known patterns: Fibonacci, factorial, digit sum, reverse.

cards.title: SOLID
points: S — Single Responsibility: a class has one reason to change
O — Open/Closed: open for extension, closed for modification
L — Liskov Substitution: subclasses must work wherever the parent is expected
I — Interface Segregation: many small interfaces beat one fat one
D — Dependency Inversion: depend on abstractions, not concrete classes

cards.title: SRP and DIP together
cards.body: An Invoice class that calculates totals, prints PDFs and emails customers has three reasons to change. Split it into Invoice, InvoicePrinter and InvoiceMailer. Give the mailer a Notifier interface in its constructor, so EmailNotifier or SmsNotifier can be plugged in without editing it (dependency injection).

cards.title: Liskov trap
cards.body: A Square subclass of Rectangle breaks LSP: code that sets width = 5 and height = 4 expects area 20, but a Square forces both sides equal. If substituting a subclass changes expected behaviour, the inheritance is wrong — prefer composition.

cards.title: Creational patterns
points: Singleton: exactly one instance with a global access point (config, logger)
Factory: a method decides which subclass to create
Builder: step-by-step construction of complex objects (avoids long constructors)

cards.title: Structural and behavioural patterns
points: Adapter: converts one interface into another
Decorator: adds behaviour by wrapping an object
Strategy: interchangeable algorithms behind one interface
Observer: subscribers are notified when a subject changes (events, listeners)

cards.title: MVC
cards.body: **Model** holds data and business rules, **View** displays it, **Controller** handles input and coordinates. Web frameworks (Spring MVC, Django's MTV variant, Rails) are built around it.

cards.q: A class that both stores user data and writes it to log files mainly violates:
cards.explain: It has two unrelated reasons to change.

cards.q: Choosing a payment method (card, UPI, wallet) at runtime through a common interface is the:
cards.explain: Interchangeable algorithms behind one interface.

cards.q: A newsletter that notifies all subscribers when a new issue is published follows:
cards.explain: Subscribers register and are notified on change.

notes.p: SOLID principles keep code easy to change. Interviewers ask you to name them, give an example of a violation and fix it. Tie each to a benefit: SRP keeps classes small, OCP lets you add features by adding classes, LSP keeps inheritance honest, ISP avoids forcing classes to implement methods they don't need, and DIP enables testing with mocks.

notes.h: Strategy, Factory and Observer in Java

notes.p: The classic lazy singleton is not thread-safe. In Java the simplest safe forms are an **enum singleton** (`enum Config { INSTANCE; }`) or a static holder class, which the JVM initialises lazily and safely. Singletons are global state, so they make unit testing harder — many teams prefer creating one instance and injecting it.

**Q: Composition vs inheritance?** A: Inheritance is an is-a relationship and couples the child to the parent's internals; composition (has-a) assembles behaviour from parts and is usually more flexible.

**Q: Decorator vs inheritance?** A: Decorators add behaviour at runtime by wrapping, and can be stacked (e.g. BufferedReader wrapping FileReader); inheritance fixes behaviour at compile time.

**Q: Factory vs Builder?** A: Factory picks which object to create; Builder assembles one complex object step by step.

**Q: Example of Interface Segregation?** A: Split a Machine interface with print, scan and fax into Printer, Scanner and Fax, so a basic printer implements only Printer.
Remember:
points: SRP, OCP, LSP, ISP, DIP.
Square-extends-Rectangle breaks LSP.
Depend on interfaces; inject implementations.
Singleton, Factory, Builder = creational.
Adapter, Decorator = structural.
Strategy, Observer = behavioural.
MVC separates data, display and input handling.

chapters.title: Core Java for interviews: collections, exceptions, threads, streams

cards.title: Collections at a glance
points: ArrayList: dynamic array, O(1) get, amortised O(1) add at end
LinkedList: O(1) add/remove at ends, O(n) get
HashMap: O(1) average get/put; no order. LinkedHashMap keeps insertion order; TreeMap sorted, O(log n)
HashSet uses a HashMap internally
ConcurrentHashMap for thread-safe maps (Hashtable is legacy)

cards.title: hashCode–equals contract
cards.body: If a.equals(b) then a.hashCode() == b.hashCode(). Override **both** for objects used as HashMap keys or in HashSets; otherwise two 'equal' objects land in different buckets and duplicates appear.

cards.title: HashMap internals
cards.body: An array of buckets; index from the key's hash. Collisions chain in a list, and (since Java 8) a bucket converts to a balanced tree when it holds more than 8 entries (with a large enough table). Default capacity 16, **load factor 0.75** — the table doubles when size exceeds capacity × 0.75.

cards.title: Strings and keywords
points: String immutable; StringBuilder mutable, not synchronised (fastest); StringBuffer synchronised
final: constant variable / non-overridable method / non-extendable class
finally: block that runs after try/catch (even after return)
static: belongs to the class, not instances

cards.title: Exceptions
cards.body: **Checked** exceptions (IOException, SQLException) must be caught or declared with throws. **Unchecked** (RuntimeException subclasses: NullPointerException, ArithmeticException, ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException) need not be. **Errors** (OutOfMemoryError, StackOverflowError) signal JVM problems. **try-with-resources** closes AutoCloseable resources automatically.

cards.title: Threads basics
cards.body: Create threads by extending Thread or implementing Runnable (or Callable with an ExecutorService). **synchronized** gives mutual exclusion on a monitor; **volatile** guarantees visibility of a variable across threads but not atomicity; AtomicInteger gives lock-free atomic counters.

cards.q: Which statement about Java's HashMap is true?
cards.explain: HashMap permits one null key and many null values; TreeMap sorts; Hashtable is synchronised.

cards.q: Which is a checked exception?
cards.explain: IOException must be declared or caught.

cards.q: For building a long string inside a loop in single-threaded code, the best choice is:
cards.explain: Mutable and unsynchronised.

notes.p: Each thread has its own **stack** (method frames, local primitives and references). Objects live on the shared **heap**, which the **garbage collector** reclaims when no live references point to them; modern collectors (e.g. G1, the default in recent JDKs) divide the heap into regions and collect young objects frequently. Class metadata lives in **Metaspace** (Java 8+). Deep recursion overflows the stack (StackOverflowError); leaked references fill the heap (OutOfMemoryError).

**Lambdas** (x -> x * 2) implement **functional interfaces** (one abstract method: Runnable, Comparator, Function, Predicate). **Streams** process collections declaratively: filter, map, sorted, collect; they are lazy until a terminal operation and can be parallel. **Optional** makes 'maybe absent' explicit. **Default methods** let interfaces evolve. Records (Java 16+) give concise immutable data classes; var (Java 10+) infers local types.

**Q: Interface vs abstract class?** A: A class can implement many interfaces but extend one class; abstract classes can hold state and constructors; interfaces define contracts (with default/static methods since Java 8).

**Q: Overloading vs overriding?** A: Overloading: same name, different parameters, resolved at compile time. Overriding: subclass redefines a method with the same signature, resolved at runtime.

**Q: Why is String immutable?** A: Security, string-pool sharing, safe hash keys and thread safety.

**Q: fail-fast iterator?** A: Modifying a collection during iteration (except via the iterator) throws ConcurrentModificationException.

**Q: wait() vs sleep()?** A: wait releases the monitor and needs notify; sleep pauses without releasing locks.
Remember:
points: ArrayList O(1) get; LinkedList O(1) end ops.
Override equals and hashCode together.
HashMap: buckets, load factor 0.75, treeify after 8.
StringBuilder for loops; StringBuffer if shared.
Checked must be handled; unchecked need not be.
finally runs even after return.
volatile = visibility; synchronized = mutual exclusion.

chapters.title: Core Python for interviews: data model, generators, OOP & idioms

cards.title: Everything is an object
cards.body: Names are **references** to objects. Mutable: list, dict, set, bytearray. Immutable: int, float, str, tuple, frozenset. Passing an argument passes the reference, so a function can mutate a list it receives but cannot rebind the caller's variable.

cards.title: Built-in containers
points: list: dynamic array — append O(1), insert/pop(0) O(n)
dict: hash table, O(1) average; keeps insertion order (3.7+)
set: hash set, O(1) membership
collections.deque: O(1) at both ends
collections.Counter, defaultdict for counting and grouping

cards.title: Generators
cards.body: A function with **yield** returns a generator that produces values lazily, one at a time, keeping its state between calls. Generator expressions (x*x for x in data) use O(1) memory, unlike list comprehensions. A generator can be iterated **only once**.

cards.title: Scope (LEGB)
cards.body: Names are looked up Local → Enclosing → Global → Built-in. Assigning to a name inside a function makes it local unless declared **global** (module level) or **nonlocal** (enclosing function).

cards.title: OOP essentials
points: __init__ initialises; self is the instance
@classmethod gets the class (cls); @staticmethod gets neither
Dunder methods: __str__, __repr__, __len__, __eq__, __lt__
Multiple inheritance resolves methods by the MRO (C3 linearisation)
No true private members: _name is a convention, __name is name-mangled

cards.title: The GIL
cards.body: In CPython the **Global Interpreter Lock** lets only one thread execute Python bytecode at a time. Threads still help for I/O-bound work; for CPU-bound work use multiprocessing or native extensions. (Free-threaded builds without the GIL exist experimentally in recent versions — check the current status.)

cards.q: What does print([i * i for i in range(4)][-1]) output?
cards.explain: The list is [0, 1, 4, 9]; the last element is 9.

cards.q: Which is immutable?
cards.explain: Tuples cannot be changed after creation.

cards.q: funcs = [lambda: i for i in range(3)]; print([f() for f in funcs]) prints:
cards.explain: Closures capture the variable i, not its value; after the loop i is 2 (late binding).

notes.p:
`from collections import Counter, defaultdict
def gen(n):
    for i in range(n):
        yield i * i
g = gen(4)
print(next(g), list(g), list(g))
words = 'to be or not to be'.split()
print(Counter(words).most_common(2))
groups = defaultdict(list)
for w in words: groups[len(w)].append(w)
print(dict(groups))
funcs = [lambda: i for i in range(3)]
fixed = [lambda i=i: i for i in range(3)]
print([f() for f in funcs], [f() for f in fixed])
def total(*args, **kw):
    return sum(args) * kw.get('scale', 1)
print(total(1, 2, 3), total(1, 2, scale=10))
class Point:
    count = 0
    def __init__(self, x, y): self.x, self.y = x, y; Point.count += 1
    def __repr__(self): return f'Point({self.x}, {self.y})'
    def __eq__(self, o): return (self.x, self.y) == (o.x, o.y)
    @classmethod
    def origin(cls): return cls(0, 0)
print(Point(1, 2), Point(1, 2) == Point(1, 2), Point.origin(), Point.count)
try:
    {}['missing']
except KeyError as e:
    print('KeyError', e)
else:
    print('no error')
finally:
    print('cleanup')
print(sorted(['banana', 'Apple', 'cherry'], key=str.lower), {k: v for k, v in zip('abc', range(3))})`

Output:
`0 [1, 4, 9] []
[('to', 2), ('be', 2)]
{2: ['to', 'be', 'or', 'to', 'be'], 3: ['not']}
[2, 2, 2] [0, 1, 2]
6 30
Point(1, 2) True Point(0, 0) 4
KeyError 'missing'
cleanup
['Apple', 'banana', 'cherry'] {'a': 0, 'b': 1, 'c': 2}`

The generator is exhausted after the first list() call, so the second gives []. The default-argument trick (i=i) captures each value and fixes the late-binding lambdas.

An **iterator** implements __iter__ and __next__ and raises StopIteration at the end; for-loops use this protocol. A **context manager** (with open(...) as f) guarantees cleanup through __enter__/__exit__, even on exceptions. A **decorator** wraps a function: @functools.lru_cache memoises, @property turns a method into an attribute, and custom decorators add logging or timing. Use functools.wraps so the wrapped function keeps its name.

notes.h: Worked example: choosing the right structure
notes.p:
Task: given 10⁶ log lines, report the 3 most frequent IP addresses.
Naive: a list and list.count() per IP → O(n²).
Better: Counter(ip for line in lines) then most_common(3) → **O(n)** counting plus a heap for top-k.
If the file does not fit in memory, iterate the file object line by line (it is itself a lazy iterator) instead of calling readlines().

**Q: is vs ==?** A: is checks identity (same object); == checks equality (__eq__).

**Q: Why use a tuple as a dict key but not a list?** A: Keys must be hashable; lists are mutable and unhashable.

**Q: What is a list comprehension vs a generator expression?** A: [..] builds the whole list now; (..) yields lazily.

**Q: __str__ vs __repr__?** A: __str__ is for users (print); __repr__ is unambiguous for developers and used by the REPL and containers.

**Q: How are arguments passed?** A: By object reference ('call by sharing').

**Q: What does if __name__ == '__main__' do?** A: Runs code only when the file is executed directly, not when imported.
Remember:
points: Mutable: list, dict, set; immutable: int, str, tuple.
dict keeps insertion order; set/dict lookups O(1).
Generators are lazy and single-use.
LEGB lookup; global/nonlocal to rebind.
Late-binding closures: use default args.
@classmethod gets cls; @staticmethod gets nothing.
GIL: threads for I/O, processes for CPU.

cards.title: What Big-O means
cards.body: Big-O is an upper bound on how running time grows with input size n. Drop constants and lower-order terms: 3n² + 5n + 2 → O(n²).

cards.title: Growth order
points: O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n²) < O(2ⁿ) < O(n!)

cards.title: Counting loops
Space complexity
cards.body: Extra memory used as n grows. Recursion uses stack space: recursive factorial is O(n) space even though it stores no array.

cards.title: Best, average, worst, amortised
cards.body: Quick sort: O(n log n) average, O(n²) worst. Appending to a dynamic array (ArrayList, Python list) is O(1) amortised — an occasional O(n) resize is spread over many appends.

cards.title: Common recurrences
points: T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1) → O(log n)  (binary search)
T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) → O(n log n)  (merge sort)

cards.title: Fit the constraints
cards.body: ~10⁸ simple operations ≈ 1 second. n ≤ 10⁵ needs O(n log n) or better; n ≤ 10³ allows O(n²); n ≤ 20 allows O(2ⁿ).

cards.q:
for (i = 1; i < n; i = i * 2)
  for (j = 0; j < n; j++)  — complexity?
cards.explain: Outer loop runs log n times, inner loop n times each.

cards.q: T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1) solves to:
cards.explain: The problem halves each step with constant work: log n levels.

cards.q: With n = 10⁵, which algorithm is likely too slow for a 1-second limit?
cards.explain: 10¹⁰ operations is far beyond ~10⁸ per second.

notes.p:
**Time complexity** describes how the number of basic steps grows as the input size **n** grows. **Big-O** gives an upper bound on that growth and ignores constants and smaller terms: 3n² + 5n + 20 is **O(n²)**. **Space complexity** measures extra memory used (not counting the input itself, unless asked).

Related notations: **Ω (Omega)** is a lower bound, **Θ (Theta)** is a tight bound (both upper and lower). In interviews 'complexity' usually means worst-case Big-O.

Growth order from fastest to slowest algorithm: **O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n²) < O(n³) < O(2ⁿ) < O(n!)**. A useful rule: about 10⁸ simple operations run in roughly one second, so for n = 10⁵ an O(n²) solution (10¹⁰ steps) will time out, but O(n log n) is fine.

Single loop to n → O(n). Two **nested** loops each to n → O(n²). A loop that **doubles or halves** its variable (`i *= 2`) runs about log₂ n times → O(log n). Two loops **one after another** add: O(n) + O(m) = O(n + m). A triangle loop (`j` from `i` to n) still does n(n + 1)/2 steps → O(n²).

Let's count actual steps for n = 16:

`def count_ops(n):
    square = sum(1 for i in range(n) for j in range(n))
    log_steps, i = 0, 1
    while i < n:
        i *= 2
        log_steps += 1
    triangle = sum(1 for i in range(n) for j in range(i, n))
    return square, log_steps, triangle

print(count_ops(16))
print(count_ops(1024)[1])`

Output:
`(256, 4, 136)
10`

256 = 16², 4 = log₂ 16, and 136 = 16 × 17/2. Even though the triangle loop does about half the work of the square loop, both are **O(n²)**.

For recursion, write a **recurrence**. Binary search: T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1) → O(log n). Merge sort: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) → O(n log n). Naive Fibonacci: T(n) = T(n − 1) + T(n − 2) + O(1) → about O(2ⁿ) (more precisely O(1.618ⁿ)). Recursion also uses **stack space** equal to its maximum depth, so naive Fibonacci needs O(n) space.

**Amortised analysis:** appending to a Python list or Java ArrayList is O(1) amortised. Occasionally the array is resized (O(n)), but averaged over many appends each costs constant time.
points: Hash map get/put: O(1) average, O(n) worst case.
Sorting (merge, heap, Timsort): O(n log n).
BFS/DFS on a graph: O(V + E).
Balanced BST search: O(log n); skewed BST: O(n).
Generating all subsets: O(2ⁿ); all permutations: O(n!).

notes.p:
**Q: What is the complexity of `for (i = 1; i < n; i = i * 3)`?** A: O(log₃ n), which is O(log n) since log bases differ by a constant.

**Q: Is O(2n) different from O(n)?** A: No, constants are dropped.

**Q: Why is quicksort O(n²) in the worst case?** A: If the pivot is always the smallest or largest element (e.g. sorted input with first-element pivot), partitions are of size n − 1 and 0.

**Q: What is the space complexity of merge sort?** A: O(n) extra for the merge arrays (plus O(log n) recursion stack).

**Q: Best, average, worst case — which matters?** A: Worst case gives a guarantee; average matters for practical speed (quicksort is O(n log n) on average).
Common mistakes in complexity answers:
points: Saying a loop inside a loop is always O(n²) — the inner loop might run log n times, giving O(n log n).
Forgetting the cost of built-ins: `x in list` is O(n), `list.insert(0, x)` is O(n), string concatenation in a loop can be O(n²).
Ignoring recursion stack space.
Mixing up n and the number of digits (for number problems, input size is often log n).

notes.p: Remember:
points: Drop constants and lower-order terms.
1 < log n < n < n log n < n² < 2ⁿ < n!.
Halving/doubling loops → log n.
Sequential blocks add; nested blocks multiply.
≈10⁸ operations per second as a sanity check.
Recursion: write T(n) and count stack depth for space.
Hash map O(1) average; sorting O(n log n).

cards.title: Arrays
cards.body: Contiguous memory: O(1) access by index, O(n) insert/delete in the middle (elements shift). Most placement coding questions start here.

cards.title: Prefix sums
cards.body: pre[i] = pre[i−1] + a[i]. Any range sum a[l..r] = pre[r] − pre[l−1] in O(1) after O(n) preprocessing.

cards.title: Two pointers on a sorted array
Sliding window
cards.body: For 'best subarray of size k' or 'longest window satisfying a condition', slide a window: add the new element, remove the old one. O(n) instead of O(n·k).

cards.title: Kadane's algorithm
cards.body:
Maximum subarray sum:
cur = best = a[0]
for x in a[1:]:
    cur = max(x, cur + x)
    best = max(best, cur)
For [−2,1,−3,4,−1,2,1,−5,4] → 6 (subarray 4,−1,2,1).

cards.title: Frequently asked
cards.body: Reverse an array, move zeros to the end, second largest, rotate by k, missing number (n(n+1)/2 − sum), duplicates, merge two sorted arrays, leaders in an array.

cards.q: Find the missing number in an array holding 1..n with one value missing. Best approach?
options: Sum (or XOR) trick: O(n) time, O(1) space
Sort then scan: O(n log n)
Binary search on unsorted array: O(log n)
cards.explain: Expected sum n(n+1)/2 minus actual sum gives the missing value in one pass.

cards.q: Kadane's algorithm on [2, −1, 3, −4, 5] gives:
Time complexity of the two-pointer pair-sum on a sorted array:
cards.explain: Each step moves one pointer inward; at most n steps.

notes.p:
An **array** stores elements in contiguous memory, so reading `a[i]` is **O(1)**, but inserting or deleting in the middle is **O(n)** because elements must shift. Most array interview problems can be solved with one of four patterns: **prefix sums**, **two pointers**, **sliding window** and **Kadane's algorithm**.

**Prefix sum:** `pre[i]` = sum of the first i elements. The sum of a[l..r] = `pre[r + 1] − pre[l]` in O(1) after O(n) preprocessing.

**Two pointers:** on a **sorted** array, put `left` at the start and `right` at the end. If the sum is too small, move left forward; if too big, move right backward. This finds a pair with a target sum in O(n) instead of O(n²).

**Sliding window:** keep a window of size k and slide it by adding the new element and removing the old one, instead of recomputing the sum each time.

`def pair_with_sum(a, target):          # a is sorted
    l, r = 0, len(a) - 1
    while l < r:
        s = a[l] + a[r]
        if s == target:
            return l, r
        if s < target:
            l += 1
        else:
            r -= 1
    return None

def prefix(a):
    pre = [0]
    for x in a:
        pre.append(pre[-1] + x)
    return pre

def kadane(a):
    best = cur = a[0]
    for x in a[1:]:
        cur = max(x, cur + x)
        best = max(best, cur)
    return best

def max_window(a, k):
    s = best = sum(a[:k])
    for i in range(k, len(a)):
        s += a[i] - a[i - k]
        best = max(best, s)
    return best

print(pair_with_sum([1, 2, 4, 7, 11, 15], 15))
pre = prefix([3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9])
print(pre, pre[4] - pre[1])
print(kadane([-2, 1, -3, 4, -1, 2, 1, -5, 4]))
print(max_window([2, 1, 5, 1, 3, 2], 3))`

Output:
`(2, 4)
[0, 3, 4, 8, 9, 14, 23] 6
6
9`

Kadane's idea: at each element, either extend the previous subarray or start fresh, whichever is larger. The best subarray here is [4, −1, 2, 1] with sum 6.

All four functions above run in **O(n) time**. Two pointers, Kadane and sliding window use **O(1) extra space**; prefix sums use O(n) for the extra array. Compare with brute force: checking every pair is O(n²) and every subarray sum is O(n²) even with clever loops (O(n³) if summed naively).

**Q: Two-sum on an unsorted array?** A: Use a hash map of value → index: for each x, check if target − x is already in the map. O(n) time, O(n) space.

**Q: Move all zeros to the end keeping order.** A: Keep a write pointer; copy non-zeros forward, then fill the rest with zeros. O(n), O(1) space.

**Q: Find the missing number in 1..n.** A: n(n + 1)/2 minus the array sum, or XOR of all indices and values.

**Q: Rotate an array by k.** A: Reverse the whole array, then reverse the first k and the remaining n − k parts (k taken mod n).

**Q: Count subarrays with sum k (with negatives).** A: Prefix sums plus a hash map counting how often each prefix sum appeared.
Edge cases interviewers check:
points: Empty array or a single element.
All negative numbers in Kadane (answer is the largest single element, not 0).
Two pointers only works directly on sorted data.
Off-by-one in prefix sums (pre has n + 1 entries).
k larger than the array length in sliding window.

notes.p: Patterns to remember:
points: Range sum → prefix sums.
Sorted + pair/triplet → two pointers.
Fixed or variable window → sliding window.
Max subarray → Kadane.
Unsorted pair lookup → hash map.
Aim for O(n) time, O(1) space where possible.

cards.title: Strings are immutable
cards.body: In Java and Python, s += c inside a loop copies the string every time (O(n²)). Use StringBuilder in Java or ''.join(list) in Python.

cards.title: Hash maps & sets
cards.body: Average O(1) insert, delete and lookup; worst case O(n) when many keys collide. The go-to tool for counting, duplicates and 'have I seen this?'.

cards.title: Two Sum with a hash map
Anagram check
Palindrome
cards.body: Two pointers from both ends moving inward; skip non-alphanumerics if the question says so. O(n) time, O(1) space.

cards.title: Longest substring without repeats
cards.body: Sliding window + map of last-seen index. When a repeat appears inside the window, move the left edge past its previous position. O(n).

cards.title: First non-repeating character
cards.body: Pass 1: count frequencies. Pass 2: return the first character with count 1. Two linear passes beat any nested loop.

cards.q: Length of the longest substring without repeating characters in "abcabcbb":
cards.explain: "abc" is the longest window with distinct characters.

cards.q: Average-case lookup time in a hash table:
cards.explain: Hashing jumps straight to the bucket; collisions make the worst case O(n).

cards.q: First non-repeating character in "swiss":
cards.explain: Counts: s=3, w=1, i=1. Scanning left to right, w comes first.

notes.h: Strings and hash maps go together
notes.p:
A string is a sequence of characters. In Java and Python strings are **immutable**: every change creates a new string, so building a long string with `+=` in a loop can cost O(n²). Use `StringBuilder` in Java or `''.join(list)` in Python.

A **hash map** (Python `dict`, Java `HashMap`) stores key–value pairs. A **hash function** turns the key into an array index. When two keys land on the same index we have a **collision**, handled by **chaining** (a list per bucket) or **open addressing** (probe the next slot). When the **load factor** (items/buckets) passes a threshold (0.75 in Java's HashMap), the table is resized. Average get/put is **O(1)**; worst case with many collisions is O(n).

Most string interview questions reduce to **counting characters** (a frequency map) or a **sliding window** with a map that remembers the last position of each character.

`is_anagram`, `first_unique` and `is_palindrome` run in **O(n)** time. `longest_unique` is also **O(n)** because each index is visited once and `start` only moves forward. Space is O(k), where k is the number of distinct characters (at most 26 for lowercase letters, so effectively O(1)). Sorting both strings is an alternative anagram check in O(n log n).

**Q: Group a list of words into anagram groups.** A: Use a dict whose key is the sorted word (or a 26-count tuple); append each word to its key's list. O(n · k log k).

**Q: Why must keys in a hash map be immutable?** A: If a key changes after insertion its hash changes and the map can no longer find it.

**Q: What happens if two keys have the same hashCode in Java?** A: They go into the same bucket; `equals()` distinguishes them. Java 8+ converts long chains into balanced trees.

**Q: Reverse the words in a sentence.** A: Split on spaces, reverse the list, join with spaces: `' '.join(s.split()[::-1])`.

**Q: Check if one string is a rotation of another.** A: Same length and `b in a + a`.
Watch out for:
points: Case and spaces in anagram/palindrome questions — clarify the rules first.
Unicode vs ASCII assumptions (an array of 26 counts only works for a–z).
Concatenating strings in a loop (quadratic time).
In Java, comparing strings with `==` instead of `.equals()`.

notes.p: Remember:
points: Strings are immutable; use join/StringBuilder.
Hash map: O(1) average, O(n) worst.
Collisions: chaining or open addressing; resize at a load factor.
Frequency map solves anagram/unique questions.
Sliding window + last-seen map for 'longest substring' questions.
Rotation check: b in a + a.

cards.title: Structure
cards.body: Each node stores data and a pointer to the next node. O(1) insert/delete at a known node, O(n) access by index. Variants: singly, doubly, circular.

cards.title: Reverse a list (iterative)
cards.body:
def reverse(head):
    prev = None
    while head:
        nxt = head.next
        head.next = prev
        prev, head = head, nxt
    return prev
O(n) time, O(1) space — the most-asked linked-list question.

cards.title: Fast & slow pointers
cards.body: Slow moves 1 step, fast moves 2. When fast hits the end, slow is at the middle. If they ever meet, the list has a cycle (Floyd's algorithm).

cards.title: Merge two sorted lists
cards.body: Use a dummy head and a tail pointer; repeatedly attach the smaller front node. O(n + m).

cards.title: Remove n-th node from end
cards.body: Move fast n steps ahead, then move both until fast reaches the end; slow is just before the node to delete. One pass.

cards.title: Dummy node
cards.body: A dummy node before the head removes special cases for deleting or inserting at the head. Return dummy.next at the end.

cards.q: Floyd's cycle detection relies on:
options: Two pointers moving at different speeds
A hash of every node's value
cards.explain: If a cycle exists, the fast pointer eventually meets the slow one inside it.

cards.q: Time to access the k-th element of a singly linked list:
cards.explain: You must walk k nodes from the head.

cards.q: Slow moves 1 step, fast moves 2. When fast reaches the end, slow points to:
cards.explain: Fast covers twice the distance of slow.

notes.h: Structure and when to use it
notes.p:
A **linked list** is a chain of **nodes**; each node stores data and a pointer to the **next** node. The list is accessed through its **head**. In a **doubly linked list** each node also points to the previous node; in a **circular list** the last node points back to the head.

Compared with arrays: insertion/deletion at a known node is **O(1)** (just relink pointers), but access by index is **O(n)** because you must walk from the head. Linked lists also have no wasted capacity but use extra memory for pointers and have poor cache locality.

Three tricks solve most problems: **dummy head node** (simplifies edge cases), **fast and slow pointers** (middle, cycle detection) and **in-place reversal** with three pointers (prev, curr, next).

Reverse, middle, cycle detection: **O(n) time, O(1) space**. Merging two sorted lists of sizes m and n: **O(m + n) time, O(1) extra space** (nodes are relinked, not copied). A recursive reverse also works but uses O(n) stack space.

**Q: Delete a node when you only have a pointer to it (not the head).** A: Copy the next node's value into it and bypass the next node. Not possible for the last node.

**Q: Find the nth node from the end in one pass.** A: Move a lead pointer n steps ahead, then move both until the lead reaches the end.

**Q: Find where a cycle starts.** A: After slow and fast meet, reset one pointer to head and move both one step at a time; they meet at the cycle start.

**Q: Array vs linked list?** A: Array: O(1) index access, cache-friendly, costly inserts. Linked list: O(1) insert/delete at a known node, O(n) access.

**Q: Check if a list is a palindrome in O(1) space.** A: Find the middle, reverse the second half, compare, then restore.
Common bugs:
points: Losing the rest of the list by overwriting `next` before saving it.
Not handling an empty list or a single node.
Forgetting to return the new head after reversal.
Null pointer access when checking `fast.next.next` without checking `fast.next`.

notes.p: Remember:
points: Access O(n); insert/delete at a known node O(1).
Dummy node removes head-special cases.
Fast/slow pointers: middle and cycle.
Reverse with prev, curr, next.
nth from end: two pointers n apart.
Merge sorted lists by relinking nodes.

cards.title: Stack (LIFO)
cards.body: push, pop, peek in O(1). Used for function calls, undo, bracket matching, expression evaluation, DFS and backtracking.

cards.title: Queue (FIFO)
cards.body: enqueue at rear, dequeue at front, O(1). Variants: circular queue, deque (both ends), priority queue (heap, O(log n) insert/remove). BFS uses a queue.

cards.title: Balanced brackets
Postfix evaluation
cards.body: Scan left to right; push numbers; on an operator pop two, apply, push the result. "2 3 4 * +" → push 2, 3, 4; * → 12; + → 14.

cards.title: Monotonic stack
cards.body: Next greater element for every index in O(n): keep a stack of indices with decreasing values; when a bigger value arrives, it is the answer for everything it pops.

cards.title: Classic conversions
cards.body: Queue using two stacks (amortised O(1)), stack using queues, min-stack with an auxiliary stack.

cards.q: Evaluate the postfix expression: 5 1 2 + 4 * + 3 −
Breadth-first search uses which data structure?
cards.explain: BFS visits nodes level by level, first-in first-out.

cards.q: Push 1, 2, 3; pop; push 4; pop. The popped values in order are:
cards.explain: LIFO: first pop removes 3; after pushing 4, the next pop removes 4.

notes.p:
A **stack** is **Last In, First Out (LIFO)**: push and pop happen at the top, both O(1). Real uses: function call stack, undo, browser back button, matching brackets, expression evaluation.

A **queue** is **First In, First Out (FIFO)**: enqueue at the rear, dequeue at the front. Real uses: printer jobs, CPU scheduling, BFS. A **deque** allows both ends; a **priority queue** (heap) always removes the smallest (or largest) element in O(log n).

In Python use a list as a stack (`append`, `pop`) and `collections.deque` as a queue (`append`, `popleft`). Do not use `list.pop(0)` for queues: it is O(n). In Java prefer `ArrayDeque` for both.

notes.h: Code: brackets, next greater element, postfix

notes.p: Push, pop, enqueue, dequeue: **O(1)**. Bracket matching and postfix evaluation: **O(n)** time and O(n) space in the worst case. Next greater element: **O(n)** total even though there is a while loop inside the for loop, because every element is popped at most once (amortised argument).

**Q: Implement a queue using two stacks.** A: Push into `in`; to dequeue, if `out` is empty move everything from `in` to `out`, then pop `out`. Amortised O(1).

**Q: Design a stack that returns the minimum in O(1).** A: Keep a second stack where each entry stores the minimum so far; push/pop both together.

**Q: Stack overflow — what is it?** A: The call stack runs out of space, usually from very deep or infinite recursion.

**Q: Where is a circular queue useful?** A: Fixed-size buffers (e.g. streaming data); it reuses empty slots at the front by wrapping indices with mod.

**Q: Convert infix `a + b * c` to postfix.** A: `a b c * +` (multiplication has higher precedence).
Avoid these:
points: Popping from an empty stack — always check first.
Operand order in postfix: for `a b -`, pop b first, then a, and compute a − b.
Using a Python list as a queue (`pop(0)` is O(n)).
Forgetting that a stack being empty at the end is required for balanced brackets.

notes.p: Remember:
points: Stack = LIFO, queue = FIFO.
Brackets, undo, recursion, postfix → stack.
BFS, scheduling, buffering → queue.
Monotonic stack for next greater/smaller.
Queue from two stacks: amortised O(1).
Python: list for stack, deque for queue.

cards.title: Anatomy of recursion
cards.body: Every recursive function needs a base case (stops) and a recursive case that moves towards it. Missing base case → stack overflow.

cards.title: Naive Fibonacci
Recursion tree
cards.body: Draw calls as a tree to count work: number of nodes × work per node. Depth of the tree = stack space used.

cards.title: Backtracking pattern
cards.body: Choose → explore → un-choose. Build a partial solution, recurse, then undo the last choice to try the next one. Used for subsets, permutations, N-Queens, Sudoku, word search.

cards.title: All subsets
Output sizes
points: Subsets of n items: 2ⁿ
Permutations of n distinct items: n!
So these problems are only feasible for small n (≈ 20 for subsets, ≈ 10 for permutations)

cards.q: How many subsets does {a, b, c, d} have?
cards.explain: 2⁴ = 16, including the empty set.

cards.q: Space complexity of recursive factorial(n):
cards.explain: n stack frames are alive at the deepest point.

notes.p:
A **recursive** function solves a problem by calling itself on a **smaller** version of the same problem. Every recursive function needs (1) a **base case** that stops the recursion and (2) a **recursive case** that moves toward the base case. Without a reachable base case you get infinite recursion and a **stack overflow**.

Each call is pushed on the **call stack** with its own local variables. So `factorial(5)` keeps five frames alive at the deepest point: recursion depth = extra space. Python's default recursion limit is about 1000 frames.

Think of recursion as trust: assume `f(n − 1)` already works, then just describe how to build `f(n)` from it.

**Backtracking** builds a solution step by step and **undoes** a choice when it leads to a dead end. The template is: for each option — make the choice, recurse, then remove the choice. It is used for subsets, permutations, combinations, N-Queens, Sudoku and maze paths.

`def subsets(nums):
    res, cur = [], []
    def go(i):
        if i == len(nums):
            res.append(cur[:])
            return
        cur.append(nums[i]); go(i + 1); cur.pop()   # take nums[i]
        go(i + 1)                                    # skip nums[i]
    go(0)
    return res

def permutations(s):
    if len(s) <= 1:
        return [s]
    return [s[i] + p for i in range(len(s)) for p in permutations(s[:i] + s[i + 1:])]

def n_queens(n):
    cols, d1, d2 = set(), set(), set()
    def place(r):
        if r == n:
            return 1
        count = 0
        for c in range(n):
            if c in cols or r - c in d1 or r + c in d2:
                continue
            cols.add(c); d1.add(r - c); d2.add(r + c)
            count += place(r + 1)
            cols.remove(c); d1.remove(r - c); d2.remove(r + c)
        return count
    return place(0)

print(subsets([1, 2, 3]))
print(permutations("abc"))
print(n_queens(4), n_queens(8))`

Output:
`[[1, 2, 3], [1, 2], [1, 3], [1], [2, 3], [2], [3], []]
['abc', 'acb', 'bac', 'bca', 'cab', 'cba']
2 92`

In N-Queens, a queen attacks along its column, its main diagonal (r − c is constant) and its anti-diagonal (r + c is constant). Sets make each safety check O(1).

Subsets: 2ⁿ subsets, each copied in O(n) → **O(n · 2ⁿ)** time, O(n) recursion depth. Permutations: n! results of length n → **O(n · n!)**. N-Queens is exponential but **pruning** (skipping unsafe squares early) makes it far faster than trying all n^n placements. Factorial and sum-of-digits recursion are O(n) time and O(n) stack space.

**Q: Recursion vs iteration?** A: Recursion is often clearer for tree-shaped problems but uses stack space and has call overhead; iteration avoids stack overflow.

**Q: What is tail recursion?** A: The recursive call is the last operation, so a compiler can reuse the frame. Java and Python do not optimise it.

**Q: How do you avoid duplicate subsets when input has duplicates?** A: Sort the input and skip an element equal to the previous one at the same recursion level.

**Q: How is backtracking different from brute force?** A: It prunes branches as soon as a partial solution breaks a rule, instead of generating every complete candidate.

**Q: Tower of Hanoi moves for n disks?** A: 2ⁿ − 1.
Common mistakes:
points: Missing or unreachable base case.
Appending `cur` instead of a copy `cur[:]` (all results end up identical).
Forgetting to undo the choice after the recursive call.
Recomputing the same subproblem many times — that is a signal to use DP/memoisation.

notes.p: Remember:
points: Base case first, then smaller recursive call.
Depth of recursion = stack space.
Backtracking: choose → explore → un-choose.
Subsets 2ⁿ, permutations n!.
Prune early to save time.
Repeated subproblems → memoise.

cards.title: Sorting cheat-sheet
points: Bubble / selection / insertion: O(n²); insertion is O(n) on nearly sorted input
Merge sort: O(n log n) always, stable, O(n) extra space
Quick sort: O(n log n) average, O(n²) worst, in place
Heap sort: O(n log n), in place, not stable
Counting sort: O(n + k) for small integer range k

cards.title: Stability
cards.body: A stable sort keeps equal keys in their original order — needed when sorting by a second key (e.g. by marks, then keeping name order). Merge and insertion sort are stable.

cards.title: Binary search
cards.body:
def bsearch(a, x):
    lo, hi = 0, len(a) - 1
    while lo <= hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if a[mid] == x: return mid
        if a[mid] < x: lo = mid + 1
        else: hi = mid - 1
    return -1
O(log n), array must be sorted.

cards.title: Binary search on the answer
cards.body: If 'can we do it with value X?' is monotonic (false…false, true…true), binary search X. Used for integer square root, minimum capacity, allocate books, aggressive cows.

cards.title: Overflow-safe mid
cards.body: In C/Java write mid = lo + (hi − lo) / 2; (lo + hi) can overflow int for large indices.

cards.title: First/last occurrence
cards.body: On a match, don't stop: record the index and continue left (hi = mid − 1) for the first occurrence or right (lo = mid + 1) for the last.

cards.q: Worst-case time complexity of quick sort:
cards.explain: Happens with consistently bad pivots, e.g. already-sorted input with first-element pivot.

cards.q: Which of these sorting algorithms is stable?
cards.explain: Merge sort preserves the order of equal keys; the others (standard versions) do not.

cards.q: Binary search requires the input to be:
cards.explain: The halving logic depends on sorted order.

notes.p: You should know how each sort works and its complexity. **Stable** means equal elements keep their original order.
points: **Bubble sort:** swap adjacent out-of-order pairs; O(n²), best O(n) with early exit; stable.
**Selection sort:** pick the minimum each pass; O(n²) always; not stable; fewest swaps.
**Insertion sort:** insert each element into the sorted left part; O(n²), O(n) on nearly sorted data; stable.
**Merge sort:** split, sort halves, merge; O(n log n) always; O(n) extra space; stable.
**Quick sort:** partition around a pivot; O(n log n) average, O(n²) worst; in-place; not stable.
**Heap sort:** build a heap, extract max repeatedly; O(n log n); O(1) space; not stable.
**Counting sort:** O(n + k) for small integer ranges k.
Python's `sorted()` and Java's object sort use **Timsort** (merge + insertion hybrid, stable, O(n log n)).

notes.h: Merge sort and binary search in code

notes.p: Binary search is not just for arrays. If the answer space is **monotonic** (if x works, every bigger x works), you can binary-search the answer. Examples: minimum speed to finish within h hours (Koko eating bananas), smallest capacity to ship packages in d days, integer square root. Each check costs O(n), so total O(n log range).

**Q: Which sort would you use for nearly sorted data?** A: Insertion sort (close to O(n)), or Timsort which exploits existing runs.

**Q: Why is quicksort often faster than merge sort in practice?** A: In-place partitioning with good cache use; random pivots make the worst case very unlikely.

**Q: Search in a rotated sorted array.** A: Modified binary search: one half is always sorted; check whether the target lies in it and discard the other half. O(log n).

**Q: Find the peak element.** A: If `a[mid] < a[mid + 1]` a peak exists on the right, else on the left. O(log n).

**Q: What does 'stable sort' matter for?** A: Sorting by multiple keys, e.g. sort by name, then stably by department keeps names ordered within each department.
Classic binary search bugs:
points: Infinite loop from `lo = mid` instead of `lo = mid + 1`.
Using `<` vs `<=` inconsistently with how hi is initialised.
Applying binary search on unsorted data.
Overflow from `(lo + hi) / 2` in C/Java.

notes.p: Remember:
points: O(n²): bubble, selection, insertion.
O(n log n): merge (stable, O(n) space), heap (in-place), quick (average).
Quick sort worst case O(n²) with bad pivots.
Binary search: sorted input, O(log n).
First/last occurrence: keep searching after a match.
Binary search on answer for monotonic conditions.

cards.title: Vocabulary
cards.body: Root, parent, child, leaf, height (longest root-to-leaf path), depth. A binary tree of height h (root at height 0) has at most 2^(h+1) − 1 nodes.

cards.title: Traversals
points: Inorder: Left, Node, Right
Preorder: Node, Left, Right
Postorder: Left, Right, Node
Level order: BFS with a queue

cards.title: Recursive inorder & height
Binary search tree
cards.body: Left subtree < node < right subtree. Inorder traversal gives sorted order. Search/insert cost O(h): O(log n) if balanced, O(n) if skewed (e.g. inserting sorted data).

cards.title: Build and traverse
cards.body:
Insert 50, 30, 70, 20, 40 into an empty BST.
Preorder: 50 30 20 40 70
Inorder: 20 30 40 50 70
Postorder: 20 40 30 70 50

cards.title: Balanced trees & heaps
cards.body: AVL and red-black trees self-balance to keep O(log n). A heap is a complete binary tree (stored in an array) where each parent ≤ children (min-heap).

cards.q: Inorder traversal of a BST visits keys in:
cards.explain: Left < node < right, visited in that order.

cards.q: Postorder of the BST built by inserting 50, 30, 70, 20, 40:
cards.explain: Left subtree (20 40 30), right subtree (70), then root 50.

cards.q: Worst-case search time in an unbalanced BST with n nodes:
cards.explain: A skewed BST degenerates into a linked list.

notes.p:
A **tree** is a hierarchical structure of nodes with one **root** and no cycles. A **binary tree** gives each node at most two children (left and right). **Leaf**: node with no children. **Height**: number of edges (or nodes, depending on the book — say which you use) on the longest root-to-leaf path. A binary tree of height h (counting levels) has at most 2ʰ − 1 nodes.

A **binary search tree (BST)** keeps the rule: every value in the **left subtree is smaller** and every value in the **right subtree is larger** than the node. That makes search, insert and delete **O(h)**: O(log n) if balanced, but **O(n)** if the tree becomes a skewed chain (e.g. inserting sorted data). **AVL** and **red-black trees** rebalance automatically to keep O(log n).

Traversals: **inorder** (left, root, right) — gives sorted order for a BST; **preorder** (root, left, right) — used to copy/serialise trees; **postorder** (left, right, root) — used to delete trees; **level order** — BFS with a queue.

notes.h: Code: build a BST and traverse it
notes.p:
`from collections import deque

class Node:
    def __init__(self, v):
        self.v, self.left, self.right = v, None, None

def insert(root, v):
    if root is None:
        return Node(v)
    if v < root.v:
        root.left = insert(root.left, v)
    else:
        root.right = insert(root.right, v)
    return root

def inorder(n):   return inorder(n.left) + [n.v] + inorder(n.right) if n else []
def preorder(n):  return [n.v] + preorder(n.left) + preorder(n.right) if n else []
def postorder(n): return postorder(n.left) + postorder(n.right) + [n.v] if n else []
def height(n):    return 1 + max(height(n.left), height(n.right)) if n else 0

def level_order(root):
    out, q = [], deque([root])
    while q:
        level = []
        for _ in range(len(q)):
            n = q.popleft()
            level.append(n.v)
            q.extend(c for c in (n.left, n.right) if c)
        out.append(level)
    return out

def lca(n, a, b):          # lowest common ancestor in a BST
    while n:
        if a < n.v and b < n.v: n = n.left
        elif a > n.v and b > n.v: n = n.right
        else: return n.v

root = None
for v in [50, 30, 70, 20, 40, 60, 80]:
    root = insert(root, v)
print(inorder(root))
print(preorder(root))
print(postorder(root))
print(level_order(root), height(root))
print(lca(root, 20, 40), lca(root, 20, 60))`

Output:
`[20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80]
[50, 30, 20, 40, 70, 60, 80]
[20, 40, 30, 60, 80, 70, 50]
[[50], [30, 70], [20, 40, 60, 80]] 3
30 50`

Every traversal visits each node once: **O(n) time**, O(h) recursion space (O(n) for level order's queue in the worst case). BST search/insert: **O(h)** — O(log n) balanced, O(n) skewed. The LCA function above walks one path from the root, so O(h) time and O(1) space.

**Q: How do you check if a binary tree is a valid BST?** A: Recurse with an allowed (low, high) range for each node, or check that the inorder traversal is strictly increasing. Checking only parent–child pairs is wrong.

**Q: Delete a node with two children from a BST.** A: Replace its value with the inorder successor (smallest in the right subtree), then delete that successor.

**Q: Diameter of a binary tree?** A: For each node, left height + right height; take the maximum while computing heights in one postorder pass. O(n).

**Q: Can you rebuild a tree from traversals?** A: Yes, from inorder + preorder (or inorder + postorder). Preorder + postorder alone is not enough for a general binary tree.

**Q: What is a heap and how is it different from a BST?** A: A heap only guarantees parent ≤ children (min-heap); it is a complete tree stored in an array and gives min in O(1), but not sorted order.
Watch for:
points: Skewed BST from sorted input → O(n) operations.
Validating a BST by comparing only immediate children.
Height definitions: edges vs nodes.
Duplicate values — decide whether they go left or right.

notes.p: Remember:
points: BST: left < node < right.
Inorder of a BST = sorted.
Pre = root first, post = root last, level = queue.
Search/insert O(h): log n balanced, n skewed.
Validate with (low, high) bounds.
AVL/red-black keep trees balanced.

cards.title: Representation
cards.body: Adjacency matrix: O(V²) space, O(1) edge check. Adjacency list: O(V + E) space, best for sparse graphs — the default in interviews.

cards.title: BFS (shortest path, unweighted)
DFS
cards.body: Go deep using recursion or a stack. Uses: connected components, cycle detection, topological sort, path finding, flood fill. Both BFS and DFS are O(V + E).

cards.title: Topological sort
cards.body: Linear order of a DAG where every edge u→v puts u before v (task scheduling, course prerequisites). Kahn's algorithm: repeatedly remove nodes with indegree 0.

cards.title: Weighted graphs
points: Dijkstra: single-source shortest path, non-negative weights, O((V + E) log V) with a heap
Bellman-Ford: handles negative edges, detects negative cycles, O(VE)
Minimum spanning tree: Prim's or Kruskal's (with union-find)

cards.title: Grids are graphs
cards.body: 'Number of islands', 'rotten oranges', maze shortest path: each cell is a node with up to 4 neighbours. Run BFS/DFS and mark visited cells.

cards.q: Shortest path (fewest edges) in an unweighted graph is found with:
cards.explain: BFS explores in increasing distance order.

cards.q: Topological sorting is defined for:
cards.explain: A cycle makes it impossible to order every edge forward.

cards.q: Dijkstra's algorithm may give wrong answers when the graph has:
cards.explain: It assumes a finalised node can never be improved later; negative edges break that.

notes.p:
A **graph** is a set of **vertices** (V) connected by **edges** (E). Edges can be **directed** or **undirected**, **weighted** or unweighted. Two common representations: an **adjacency matrix** (V × V grid, O(V²) space, O(1) edge check) and an **adjacency list** (each vertex stores its neighbours, O(V + E) space). Interviews almost always use adjacency lists.

**BFS (breadth-first search)** explores level by level using a **queue**. It finds the **shortest path in an unweighted graph**. **DFS (depth-first search)** goes as deep as possible using **recursion or a stack**, then backtracks. DFS is used for connected components, cycle detection, topological sort and path finding.

notes.h: Code: BFS, DFS and topological sort

notes.p: BFS and DFS each visit every vertex once and look at every edge once (twice for undirected): **O(V + E) time** with an adjacency list, **O(V²)** with a matrix. Space is O(V) for the visited set and the queue/stack. Kahn's algorithm is also O(V + E).

**Q: Count islands in a grid of 0s and 1s.** A: Loop over cells; on each unvisited 1, run BFS/DFS to mark the whole island and add 1 to the count. O(rows × cols).

**Q: Detect a cycle in an undirected graph.** A: DFS; if you reach a visited vertex that is not the parent, there is a cycle (or use union-find).

**Q: Detect a cycle in a directed graph.** A: DFS with three colours (unvisited, in current path, done); an edge to an 'in path' vertex is a cycle. Or Kahn's algorithm fails to process all nodes.

**Q: Shortest path with weights?** A: Dijkstra (non-negative weights, O((V + E) log V) with a heap); Bellman-Ford handles negative weights in O(VE).

**Q: Why does BFS give shortest paths in unweighted graphs?** A: It reaches all vertices at distance k before any at distance k + 1.
Avoid:
points: Marking visited when popping instead of when pushing in BFS (causes duplicates).
Forgetting disconnected components — loop over all vertices.
Using BFS for weighted shortest paths.
Deep recursion in DFS on big graphs (use an explicit stack).

notes.p: Remember:
points: Adjacency list: O(V + E) space.
BFS = queue, levels, shortest unweighted path.
DFS = stack/recursion, components, cycles, topo sort.
Both run in O(V + E).
Topological order exists only for DAGs.
Dijkstra for non-negative weights.

cards.title: When DP applies

notes.p:
**Dynamic programming (DP)** solves problems that have (1) **overlapping subproblems** — the same smaller problem is solved again and again — and (2) **optimal substructure** — the best answer is built from best answers to smaller parts. DP stores each subproblem's answer once and reuses it.

Two styles: **memoisation (top-down)** — write the recursion and cache results; **tabulation (bottom-up)** — fill a table from the smallest cases upward. Both turn naive Fibonacci from O(2ⁿ) into **O(n)**.

Recipe for any DP problem: define the **state** (what dp[i] or dp[i][j] means), write the **transition** (how it is built from smaller states), set the **base cases**, decide the **order** of filling, and read the **answer**.

Memoised Fibonacci: O(n) time and space. 0/1 knapsack: **O(n · W)** time, O(W) space with the 1-D trick. LCS: **O(m · n)** time and space (O(min(m, n)) space if you keep only two rows). Coin change: **O(amount × coins)**. Note that O(n · W) is 'pseudo-polynomial' because W is a number, not an input length.

**Q: Climbing stairs with 1 or 2 steps — how many ways for n steps?** A: ways(n) = ways(n − 1) + ways(n − 2), which is Fibonacci; for n = 5 it is 8.

**Q: Memoisation vs tabulation?** A: Memoisation is easier to write and computes only needed states; tabulation avoids recursion depth limits and often allows space optimisation.

**Q: Why loop capacity backwards in 0/1 knapsack?** A: So each item is counted at most once; looping forwards gives the unbounded knapsack.

**Q: Longest increasing subsequence?** A: O(n²) DP with dp[i] = 1 + max dp[j] for j < i and a[j] < a[i]; O(n log n) with patience sorting and binary search.

**Q: Greedy vs DP for coins?** A: Greedy works for Indian currency denominations but fails for sets like {1, 3, 4} with amount 6 (greedy 4 + 1 + 1 = 3 coins, DP 3 + 3 = 2 coins).
Common DP mistakes:
points: Unclear state definition — write it in words first.
Wrong base case (dp[0] = 1 for counting ways, 0 for min coins).
Forward loop in 0/1 knapsack (reuses items).
Off-by-one when the table has size n + 1.

notes.p: Remember:
points: Overlapping subproblems + optimal substructure → DP.
State, transition, base case, order, answer.
Memo = top-down cache; tabulation = bottom-up table.
Knapsack O(nW); LCS O(mn); coin change O(amount × coins).
Space-optimise by keeping only needed rows.
Test greedy against DP on small counter-examples.
