**Q: Blue-green vs canary deployment?** A: Blue-green switches all traffic from the old environment to a fully deployed new one; canary sends a small percentage first and widens if metrics stay healthy.

**Q: What is IAM?** A: Identity and Access Management — users, roles and policies granting least-privilege permissions.

**Q: Essential Linux commands?** A: ls, cd, pwd, cat, less, grep, find, chmod, chown, ps, top, kill, df, du, ssh, scp, curl, tail -f for logs.
Remember:
points: IaaS (VMs) → PaaS (platform) → SaaS (software) → FaaS (functions).
Regions contain multiple availability zones.
Object vs block vs file storage.
Containers share the kernel; VMs carry a guest OS.
Docker image → container; Kubernetes orchestrates.
CI = build + test every push; CD = automated release.
Shared responsibility: provider secures the cloud, you secure what's in it.

cards.title: STAR in one line
cards.body: Answer behavioural questions ('Tell me about a time…') as Situation → Task → Action → Result. Spend most time on Action and Result.

cards.title: Each letter
points: Situation: context in 1–2 sentences
Task: your responsibility or goal
Action: what YOU did, specific steps
Result: outcome, ideally measurable, plus what you learned

cards.title: Sample answer
cards.body: S: In our final-year project, the backend teammate dropped out 3 weeks before review. T: I had to deliver the API. A: I learned Flask basics, split tasks with the team and set daily check-ins. R: We demoed on time and scored an A; I learned to plan with buffers.

cards.title: Build a story bank
cards.body: Prepare 5–6 stories that can be reused: teamwork, conflict, failure, leadership, tight deadline, learning something fast. Projects, internships, hackathons and clubs all count.

cards.title: Make it yours
cards.body: Say 'I', not just 'we'. Quantify results (reduced load time by 40%, 120 users). Keep each answer to about 1.5–2 minutes.

cards.title: Failure questions
cards.body: Pick a real but recoverable failure, own it without blaming others, and spend most of the answer on what you changed afterwards.

cards.q: In STAR, which part should usually take the most time?
cards.explain: Interviewers assess what you did; keep the setup short.

cards.q: Which is the strongest Result statement?
options: "Our app's load time fell from 5 s to 2 s and 300 students used it."
cards.explain: Specific, measurable outcomes are most convincing.

notes.h: What STAR is and why interviewers like it
notes.p:
Behavioural questions start with 'Tell me about a time when…' or 'Give an example of…'. Interviewers believe **past behaviour predicts future behaviour**, so they want a real story, not a general claim like 'I am a team player'. The **STAR method** keeps your story short and complete: **Situation, Task, Action, Result**.

**Situation** (10–15%): where and when — one or two sentences of context. **Task** (10–15%): what you were responsible for or what problem had to be solved. **Action** (50–60%): what **you** did, step by step — use 'I', not 'we'. **Result** (15–20%): what changed, ideally with a number, plus what you learned.

A good STAR answer lasts **60–90 seconds**. Longer than two minutes and the interviewer loses the thread.

**Question:** 'Tell me about a time you handled a conflict in a team.'

**Situation:** 'In my third year, four of us built a college event-registration website for our mini-project, with a two-week deadline.'

**Task:** 'Two teammates disagreed on whether to use plain PHP or a framework, and work had stopped for three days. As the person handling the database, I needed us to agree quickly.'

**Action:** 'I asked both to list what the project actually needed. I then built a tiny login page both ways in one evening and shared the time each took and the code length. We agreed on the framework because it gave built-in form validation, and I split the remaining modules so each person owned one.'

**Result:** 'We submitted two days early and scored 46 out of 50; our guide used it for the department fest, where about 300 students registered. I learned that a small experiment ends arguments faster than opinions.'
Prepare **5–6 stories** from projects, internships, hackathons, college clubs, sports or part-time work. Each story can answer several questions if you change the emphasis.
points: Teamwork or conflict.
A failure or mistake and what you learned.
Leadership or taking initiative without being asked.
Working under pressure or a tight deadline.
Learning a new technology quickly.
Handling a difficult person or feedback.

notes.h: Common questions and how to angle them
notes.p:
**Q: Tell me about a failure.** A: Choose a real but recoverable failure (missed a deadline in a hackathon), own it without blaming others, and spend most time on what you changed afterwards.

**Q: Describe a time you showed leadership.** A: Leadership can be informal: organising a study group, fixing a broken process, mentoring juniors.

**Q: Give an example of learning something fast.** A: Name the technology, the deadline, the resources you used and what you built with it.

**Q: Tell me about a time you disagreed with a teacher or manager.** A: Show respect, data and a calm discussion, and accept the final decision professionally.
Answers that score low:
points: Saying 'we' throughout, so your own role is invisible.
Spending a minute on the situation and ten seconds on the action.
No result, or a result with no number or learning.
Choosing a 'failure' that is really a boast ('I work too hard').
Memorised scripts that sound robotic — practise out loud, not word for word.

notes.p: Remember:
points: S and T short; A is the longest part.
Use 'I' for your actions.
End with a measurable result and a lesson.
Keep it to 60–90 seconds.
Prepare 5–6 flexible stories.
Be honest — follow-up questions expose made-up stories.

cards.title: Tell me about yourself
cards.body: 60–90 seconds: present (degree, key skills) → past (1–2 projects or internships) → future (why this role). Don't recite your resume line by line or share family details unless asked.

cards.title: Why this company?
cards.body: Mention something specific: its training programme (e.g. ILP, Mysuru campus, GenC), a client domain, technology focus or values — then link it to your goals.

cards.title: Strengths & weaknesses
cards.body: Strength: one quality with a proof story. Weakness: a real, non-critical one plus what you're doing about it ('I over-polish slides; I now time-box tasks').

cards.title: Logistics questions
cards.body: Relocation, shifts, service agreements or bonds: answer honestly and positively. Read the offer terms beforehand so you aren't surprised.

cards.title: Where in five years?
cards.body: Show growth within the company: strong in a technology, leading modules, maybe a certification. Avoid 'doing an MBA abroad' or 'starting my own company'.

cards.title: Ask them something
cards.body: End with a genuine question: 'What does the first year look like for freshers in this role?' or 'Which technologies does training cover?' Never ask only about salary in round one.

cards.q: Best structure for 'Tell me about yourself'?
options: Present → past → future, in about a minute
cards.explain: A short, relevant summary that ends with why you fit the role.

cards.q: Which is the best answer to 'What is your weakness?'
options: A real minor weakness plus how you are fixing it
A critical skill the job needs
cards.explain: Honesty with an improvement plan shows self-awareness.

notes.p:
In service companies the HR round is usually 10–20 minutes. HR checks **communication**, **attitude**, **honesty**, **willingness to relocate and work in shifts**, and whether you are likely to stay after training. Technical brilliance cannot rescue an arrogant or careless HR answer, so prepare as seriously as for the technical round.

Speak clearly, keep answers to about a minute, connect your answers to the company, and never contradict your resume.

notes.h: 'Tell me about yourself' — a model answer
notes.p:
Use the **present → past → future** structure and keep it under 90 seconds:

'I'm Priya, a final-year B.Tech Computer Science student from Pune with a CGPA of 8.2. Over the last two years I've focused on Java and web development; my main project is a library management app built with Spring Boot and MySQL that our college library now uses for about 500 students. I also completed a six-week internship where I wrote REST APIs and unit tests. Outside class, I coordinate our coding club's weekly contests. I'm looking to start my career in a company where I can work on real client projects and keep learning, which is why this role excites me.'

Do not repeat your full resume, and do not start with family details unless asked.

**Q: Why do you want to join our company?** A: Mention two specific, true things — its training programme, a business area or client domain, its scale — and link them to your goals. Generic praise ('it is a reputed company') sounds unprepared.

**Q: What are your strengths?** A: Pick two relevant strengths and prove each with a short example (e.g. 'I learn quickly — I picked up React in two weeks for a hackathon').

**Q: What is your weakness?** A: Name a real, non-critical weakness and the steps you are taking: 'I used to hesitate to speak in large groups, so I joined the college debate club and now present our club updates every month.'

**Q: Where do you see yourself in five years?** A: Growth inside the company: 'Strong in my technology, handling module-level responsibility and guiding juniors.'

**Q: Are you willing to relocate or work in shifts?** A: Answer honestly. Most service companies require flexibility; if you have a genuine constraint, state it politely.

**Q: Do you have any questions for us?** A: Always ask one: about the training programme, the kind of projects freshers join, or what helps new joiners succeed.

**Q: Why should we hire you?** A: Match your skills to the role in three points: technical basics, a proof of learning ability (project/internship), and attitude (teamwork, reliability).

**Q: You have a gap year/backlog — why?** A: State the fact briefly, without excuses, and show what you did to improve.

**Q: Will you leave if you get a higher offer elsewhere?** A: Focus on the long-term learning and growth you expect here; do not promise blindly or hint at leaving.

**Q: What do you know about the service bond or training agreement?** A: Read the offer terms beforehand and show you understand them.
Avoid:
points: Badmouthing your college, teachers or a previous employer.
Lying about skills — the next question will expose it.
Asking about salary or leaves as your only question.
One-word answers or very long monologues.
Inconsistent answers between the resume and the interview.

notes.p: Checklist:
points: Tell me about yourself: present → past → future, 60–90 seconds.
Research the company: business, training, recent news.
Strength + example; weakness + improvement plan.
Be honest about relocation, shifts and gaps.
Prepare one good question for the interviewer.
Dress neatly, test your camera/mic for online rounds.

cards.title: Format
cards.body: One page for freshers, clean single-column layout, readable font, PDF export. Applicant Tracking Systems (ATS) parse simple layouts better than tables and graphics.

cards.title: Section order
points: Name, phone, email, LinkedIn, GitHub
Education (CGPA / %)
Skills (languages, tools, CS subjects)
Projects
Internships / experience
Achievements, certifications, positions of responsibility

cards.title: Project bullet formula
cards.body:
Action verb + what you built + tech + impact.
✗ 'Worked on a website.'
✓ 'Built a library-booking web app in React and Flask with JWT login; used by 200+ students in my college.'

cards.title: Skills section
cards.body: List only what you can be questioned on. If you write 'Java, SQL, DSA', expect OOP, joins and a coding question on them.

cards.title: Never fake it
cards.body: Interviewers pick any line and go deep. Every project, tech and number on the page must be something you can explain and defend.

cards.title: Common mistakes
points: Objective statements full of clichés
Photos, date of birth, father's name (not needed in IT resumes)
Spelling errors and inconsistent formatting
Broken GitHub links

cards.q: Ideal resume length for a fresher applying to IT services firms:
cards.explain: Recruiters skim quickly; one focused page is standard.

cards.q: Which project line is strongest?
options: "Built a Flask expense tracker with SQLite; 50 active users"
cards.explain: It states what, how and impact.

notes.h: What recruiters look for in a fresher resume
notes.p:
A recruiter often spends **under 30 seconds** on a fresher resume, and many companies first pass it through an **ATS (applicant tracking system)** that reads keywords. Your resume must be **one page**, clean, easy to scan and honest. Every line you write can become an interview question.

Recommended order for freshers: **Header** (name, phone, professional email, LinkedIn, GitHub) → **Education** (degree, college, CGPA, year; 12th and 10th percentages) → **Skills** → **Projects** → **Internships/Experience** → **Certifications/Achievements** → **Extra-curriculars**. Skip photos, date of birth, father's name and 'Declaration' unless the company asks.

Use the formula **Action verb + what you built + technology + measurable result**. Start each bullet with a verb: built, designed, implemented, optimised, automated, reduced, led.

**Weak:** 'Worked on a website for college.'

**Strong:** 'Built a college event-registration web app using Spring Boot and MySQL; handled 300+ registrations and cut manual data entry by about 80%.'

**Weak:** 'Did an internship in Python.'

**Strong:** 'Automated weekly sales reports with Python (pandas) during a 2-month internship, reducing report time from 3 hours to 10 minutes.'

Give each project a GitHub link, and make sure the repository has a README explaining what it does and how to run it.
Group skills so they are easy to scan and only list what you can answer questions on:
points: **Languages:** Java, Python, C.
**Web:** HTML, CSS, JavaScript, React (basic).
**Databases:** MySQL, SQL queries, basic normalisation.
**Tools:** Git, GitHub, VS Code, Postman.
**CS fundamentals:** DSA, OOP, DBMS, OS, Computer Networks.
Avoid rating bars like 'Java ★★★★☆' — they mean nothing and waste space.

notes.h: Interview questions that come from your resume
notes.p:
**Q: Explain your main project.** A: Problem → your role → architecture (frontend, backend, database) → one challenge and how you solved it → result. Two minutes.

**Q: Why did you choose MySQL instead of MongoDB here?** A: Give a reason tied to the data (structured, relational, needed joins).

**Q: What would you improve in this project?** A: Shows maturity — mention testing, security (password hashing), or deployment.

**Q: You listed Python — write a function to reverse a string.** A: Be ready to code anything basic in every language you list.
Mistakes that get resumes rejected:
points: Spelling or grammar errors, or an unprofessional email ID.
Two or more pages for a fresher.
Listing technologies you have only watched videos about.
Copy-pasted 'objective' statements with no specifics.
Fancy templates with columns and graphics that ATS software cannot read.
Mismatch between resume dates/marks and the official records.

notes.p: Final checklist:
points: One page, PDF, simple single-column layout.
Education with CGPA and percentages as the company asks.
2–3 strong projects with tech stack, result and GitHub link.
Bullets: action verb + what + tech + number.
Only skills you can defend in an interview.
Proofread twice and name the file clearly (FirstName_LastName_Resume.pdf).
